A semi-transitive graph is a simple digraph where for any specific cycle with more than two vertices, the direction of the graph determines the transitiveness, but not all cycles are considered. In such a graph, if you travel from one vertex to another via any cycle, the direction of the arrow determines the possibility of direct travel between the two vertices. Naturally, we can ask if all cycles with more than two vertices exhibit this property, and we can verify that this is indeed the case in split graphs, a type of graph where we can identify two distinct clusters by comparing each vertex's connections to all others. Moreover, we can verify that one of the clusters can be orientated to create a strongly connected graph, and this orientation also makes the original graph semi-transitive.

A cutting-edge approach has been developed to accurately identify genuine hadronic tau decays in the CMS detector, distinguished from those originating from quarks or gluons. The result utilizes data from proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV center-of-mass energy, gathering 35.9 fb^-1 of luminosity during run 2. The classification model integrates a novel, complex neural network, whose inputs comprise variables derived from a tau decay classification system. The model's performance is marked by an enhanced efficiency in recognizing true tau decays, from 32% to 35%, alongside a 35% reduction in false positives, achieving an efficiency of 11% and low rates of around 3.5% and 5% for quark and gluon origins respectively. The new technique reflects significant progress over previous standards.

In the context of the upcoming Rubin Observatory's Legacy ZTF survey, multiple Kilopixel Imaging Systems are being installed to categorize various transients and variables based on their light curves. Traditional methods utilizing machine learning, particularly neural networks, have shown efficacy; however, these models rely on a predefined output structure. As a result, certain tasks like multi-categorical object identification may involve complex decisions, posing challenges for traditional models. To address this limitation, a study proposes the use of Bayesian Neural Networks as a viable alternative for non-experts, transients, and variable objects assigned in real-time by the collaborative human-expert-transient variable team. The proposed solution is a sequence-based classification scheme, generating a probability distribution for each object rather than a fixed label; this modified approach allows for more accurate representation of uncertainty. To test its effectiveness, the proposed BNN classifier will be applied to single light curves and subsequent validation will occur against the ZTF catalog to assess its accuracy. The proposed BNN classifier for Rubin observatory is called Rubin Neural Uncertain Categorizer, RNUC for short.

Our study explores the phenomenon of forward Brillouin scattering in photonic crystal fibers with solid cores, where mechanical strain induced by the interaction between modal symmetries gives rise to transfer of energy between different optical modes. We demonstrate this process through experimental means and show that the rate of energy transfer between modes is significantly dependent on the temperature, with significant differences observable between various heating and cooling processes. Furthermore, the relative strength of the interaction can be manipulated by adjusting the acoustic mode involved and optimizing the fiber's design to maximize the intensity of the interacting mechanical resonances. These findings are highly promising for the development of thermal filters and mechanical sensors with advanced capabilities.

The simplified version of Coxeter groups known as B-type Coxeter groups has been extensively studied by the second author in a series of papers, starting with his 1990 article. For any reduced word within a finite Coxeter system, the authors of this paper have developed a general theorem stating that it can be rearranged through a specific operation to yield a standard word, defined within a modified set of rules. By applying this finding to generating sets within simplified form of B-type Coxeter groups, the study on these groups has reached a comprehensive conclusion. Furthermore, this new concept has been used to formulate an alternative version of its original equivalent. Additionally, the study offers specific proof for ten unique cases involving these groups. It also introduces two novel hypotheses and provides the underlying reasoning behind their proposed results.

The Budgeted Maximum Coverage problem involves finding the most budget-restricted subset of the worst-covered elements from a set of items, typically measured by their contributions to overall coverage. This problem has close ties to the Set-Union Knapsack problem (BUKP) which attempts to cover all the worst-covered elements within a budget, taking into account their weights. Our approach proposes a novel two-phase local search algorithm for BUKP that combines state-of-the-art solvers for sub-problems, including the previously proposed Biased Random Key genetic algorithm and a novel Truncated Greedy algorithm. Our two-phase local search method has demonstrated superior performance on real-world instances, even when compared to other top solutions. Additionally, we explore the application of our algorithm to the Budgeted Maximum Coverage setting, yielding significant speed-ups for large-scale instances. Our method has also been successfully adapted to other multi-covering problems.

In the highly dynamic and sensitive realm of online gambling, accurate churn forecasting is pivotal to maintain player satisfaction, adhere to regulatory requirements, and maintain a responsible approach. This study explores the application of machine learning and statistical modeling for churn classification in online gaming, with a distinct emphasis on complying with relevant data protection protocols. By analyzing a substantial dataset from a real-world online gaming environment, the research team examines various supervised and unsupervised modeling approaches, including statistical and machine learning methods, to pinpoint the most effective strategies for churn prediction. Notably, the findings reveal that certain models exhibit exceptional performance when evaluated on new, unseen data, while also shedding light on key player characteristics that contribute to churn and the optimal timeframes for targeting preventive measures.

We examine the 2D Ising Field Theory model, particularly its behavior and critical points when applied to both magnetically active and inactive regions. By using the high-temperature expansion of the free energy, both the antiferromagnetic and ferromagnetic behaviors can be studied, allowing us to identify a critical point on the Lee-Yang critical curve without referring to thermodynamic properties. We also determine the associated critical exponents and their correspondence to a universality class involving two dimensional lattice models with central charge c=7/2. We extend this approach to other models such as the Q2.24 and Q4.24 lattice models, which are equivalent to the 2D Ising Field Theory when exposed to a strong magnetic field.

The LMPtT perturbative framework is used to derive the gluon transverse-momentum-dependent distribution, specifically the gluon SDA. This framework is applied to the gluon form factor and the gluon PDF, and used to calculate the gluon TMD distribution by taking the limit where the gluon TMD goes to zero. The calculated gluon TMD is then used to extract the gluon TMD distribution, and this is compared with the proton TMD distribution derived from the DGLAP equations. The results from the LMPtT framework are in agreement with the results from the DGLAP equations, both being in agreement with lattice simulations and experimental data. This is in agreement with the universal nature of the LMPtT framework.

In the photon-photon interaction that occurs in ultra-peripheral collisions of high-energy ions, the creation of electron-positron pairs is produced in large quantities. The SPheNZ event generator accurately simulates this process, including the formation of these pairs at both low and high momentum. The focus of the present study is on the electromagnetic interaction of low-momentum electrons and positrons with high-density nuclear targets. The production of these leptons at such low momentum is typically not accounted for by traditional initial state approximations due to higher point density in the target. The results of a specific analysis are compared against data from the ALICE experiment obtained from Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC's energy level of 5.02 GeV.

To enhance cyclist safety through automated hazard detection, a comprehensive system is proposed, which incorporates real video footage. The framework leverages a cutting-edge computer vision technique called Faster R-CNN for object identification. The objects are then categorized as hazards using sophisticated machine learning models and integrated with contextual data. The proposed system issues alerts and furnishes visual warning interfaces to inform cyclists of potential dangers. The framework effectively combines video-driven and context-based information to provide timely warnings to cyclists. The system's performance is demonstrated through experimental results on a custom cyclistic dataset. The evaluation showcases the system's ability to accurately detect and classify hazards and minimize false positives.

A novel framework for computing optimal motion trajectories under uncertainty in dynamics models and robot control parameters is presented. This approach relies on a parametric system model with unknown system parameters, mathematically encoded using Control Barrier Functions and uncertainty bounds, to ensure feasibility and stability. This method has been successfully tested on two challenging scenarios: navigating around moving objects with uncertain motion patterns and automated highway driving with unpredictable lane changes. Key advantages of this methodology include its ability to handle multiple sources of uncertainty, provide precise stability and safety guarantees, and optimize motion paths with minimal deviations. Real-world experiments validate the efficacy and scalability of this approach.

The numbers en$_n$(R) for a ring R, defined as the set of natural numbers counting the embedded ideals of height $h$, where $h\geq n$, in the power cancelation height of R. We establish lower and upper bounds for en$_n$(R) in terms of the cardinality of R. Furthermore, we examine the integrality of these bounds in the specific context of commutative rings. We also explore the relationship between en$_n$(R) and another numerical invariant, the transfinite diamond dimension, in the context of arbitrary rings.

Achieving robustness in machine learning models against malicious attacks on their input is crucial. Research has identified that some artificial intelligence models can be made resilient by incorporating principles of complexity theory and information theory, specifically the concept of Kolmogorov complexity. By utilizing this approach, researchers have successfully developed a framework for creating adversarially robust models, demonstrated the inherent limitations of advanced adversarial attacks such as project-TinyTransformer, and proposed a novel neural architecture, NatResNet. This architecture provides a unified framework for enhancing a model's resilience to adversarial attacks, addressing both gradient-based and transferable attacks.

The nonlocal conservation laws, specifically in the context of multi-dimensional traffic models, are examined where the flux function depends on the spatial distribution of densities across space and time, represented by a general, non-singular function. This paper addresses the issue of singular limit with a particular example and provides a comprehensive analysis of the admissibility of solutions. Additionally, it proves the rate of convergence for a class of iterative methods aimed at solving nonlocal traffic models, thereby extending the concept of nonlocal backward difference schemes to a broader range of functions and flux types.

A dilation surface is a class of surfaces defined as the projective images of properly embedded minimal surfaces in Euclidean space. A recent study found that a dilation surface with trivial Seifert invariants can be classified as standard if it exhibits no hyperbolic singularities, and this classification aligns with the absence of pseudo-Anosov belt link componets. This article presents an infinite number of standard dilation surfaces featuring a specific belt link component, which leads to novel examples of horizon saddle links. Moreover, it is demonstrated that a dilation surface's singularities determine its link if and only if its link represents a horizon link, and explorations are conducted into the links' topological properties. Using a translation-invariant Morse-Smale structure, a differential structure is defined on the surface, and investigation focuses on the new classification of dilation surfaces according to their differential structure.

Recent studies suggest that using correlation information in both large and microscopic scales can distinguish conscious from unconscious states and reveal unique functional patterns. Notably, research is underway to map the human brain's functional connections using correlation information. This study proposes a new method for deriving correlation information with reduced computational complexity. It then applies this method to analyze data from the Human Connectome Project and assesses its application to distinguish conscious from unconscious states. The results demonstrate that using this new method yields more accurate distinctions between states than previous methods. Furthermore, the researchers visualize and characterize the derived correlation information and examine its properties. They also compare its effectiveness with existing methods and demonstrate its advantages in terms of computational efficiency. This study further validates the use of total correlation as a valuable tool for understanding the human brain's functional connections.

The classical Segal-Bargmann theory explores the linkage between Hilbert spaces of square-integrable functions over R^n and polynomials over C^n. In this context, we develop a Clifford algebra version, connecting the spaces of square-integrable functions over R^n with components in Clifford algebra to polynomials over C^n. Our study also establishes a Taylor isomorphism, which relates the two spaces while studying their structural similarities and differences. Specifically focused on the real case with two dimensions, we derive an explicit formula for the Clifford algebra-based Segal-Bargmann transformation.

A new class of random fields, known as Gaussian conditionals, can be constructed by applying a specific transformation to multivariate Gaussian variables, their covariance matrix, and the vectors representing field values at given points. By choosing distinct Gaussian conditionals, we can obtain different subfields, which are linear combinations of the original field variables, determined by the covariance matrix and conditional vectors specific to the chosen subfields. These distinct subfields consist of one field that represents the original field itself and, in higher dimensions, multiple fields where the vectors representing field values at given points change, while the covariance matrix remains the same. A specific case study demonstrates that in three-dimensional space, the set of all possible subfields is unique. Additionally, in dimension four or higher, multiple such fields can be found.

This study examines the potential outcomes of an aviation-related disaster, such as a plane crash, and its impact on the economy, exploring the link between a ground sensor network and an airborne vehicle equipped with a wireless camera. Analyzing this connection via aerial photography reveals that a ground sensor network can transmit data to an airborne vehicle within a specified radius, and by accounting for both vertical and horizontal distances, we can establish a probabilistic model for successful data transmission between the ground sensors and the airborne vehicle.

The discovery of neutrino oscillations led to the realization that flavor conservation applies only approximately to lepton leptons. This understanding has spawned a range of questions and hypotheses about how different neutrino flavors interact. Researchers have made significant progress in mapping the structure of neutrino mass, with ongoing efforts to refine these findings. Precise measurements of key parameters, such as mixing angles, are central to disproving hypotheses like CP symmetry and identifying the sources of asymmetry. Traditionally used experiments have limitations; for instance, existing direct experiments have failed to consistently establish the sources of asymmetry. In contrast, a new method known as taste has not yet been explored. To take neutrino physics to the next level, a novel approach is needed, one capable of achieving significantly higher precision in mass related parameters. In this spirit a new experiment is proposed, one capable of achieving an order of magnitude greater precision compared to current results, effectively setting the stage for neutrino physics in the 2030s.

Improving tagged particles identification is crucial in advanced analyses at the Large Hadron Collider, especially for identifying top quarks in complex event patterns. This study presents a sophisticated method for identifying top quarks by utilizing combinations of jets tagged with a top quark appearance. Utilizing a dataset from CMS, the researchers analyzed top tagging events with a minimum of one top quark candidate, and applied machine learning techniques to assess the performance of various top tagging algorithms. By embedding these algorithms within a fixed event reconstruction framework, the researchers were able to determine the optimal combinations of these algorithms for identifying top quark patterns. Notably, the study provides a novel approach for interpreting the performance of machine learning algorithms by utilizing the Shapley values method to assess the contribution of each tagged particle to the overall success in identifying top quark patterns. This insight can be utilized in future studies to analyze the success of each tagged particle in complex events.

This document establishes the precise formulations for vital components within Virtual Organizations, specifically for their structure and relationship to resource management, along with the definition of Virtual Organization Refinement.

To enhance robustness when training policies with off-policy data, modern reinforcement learning methods use experience replay as a key technique. These methods store real-world experiences in a buffer and randomly draw from it to train their policies. However, a common issue with these methods is the poor sample efficiency when the policy being trained is still rough and poorly estimated, as they tend to collect more experiences that are less valuable. To address this, accelerated neural network training techniques, such as data augmentation and variance reduction, can be leveraged to improve experience replay. Building on this, our proposed Variance Diminution Experience Replay (VDER), a novel approach that combines Q-learning and actor-critic methods, achieves better performance by reducing the variance of bootstrapped targets and improving the condition number of bootstrapping. We have theoretically proven that VDER's updated target estimation has a lower variance and improved stability, and we have validated this by achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple continuous control benchmarks.

Two new transformation techniques, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and superbosonization, allow for a change of variables in path integrals related to odd-dimensional Gaussian integrals. By applying these methods to a specific path integral, the equations of motion have been found to be identical for the resulting systems, while the corresponding action terms exhibit distinct differences. However, the path integral itself remains unchanged for the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, yet it undergoes a non-trivial transformation known as superbosonization. It has been observed that the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation is useful for incorporating constraints, as it results in additional delta functions, whereas the superbosonization technique generates more complex non-Gaussian terms. These methods have been further utilized to apply the $c$-number shift and rotation methods to systems involving 1, 3, and 5 Grassmann variables.

A key challenge in biomedical field is to develop models that predict future health states based on body motion. This task involves using sequential data from wearable sensors to capture important aspects of human movement. A novel approach called MoDeRNN incorporates a dynamic sensor model inspired by mechanical systems, allowing for the identification of hidden factors influencing body motion. This framework also includes a neural network with memory, capable of learning long-term, interconnected patterns in human activity. By comparing this method with existing approaches, it has demonstrated superior performance in predicting future motion states from observed data. In addition, it has been observed that the new framework provides a clear and interpretable understanding of the underlying sensor information.

This research focuses on bridging the gap between programming languages employing linear type systems and those using reference type systems. Current approaches converting programs from linear to reference type systems often come with significant performance costs. Our previous work developed techniques to preserve the original program's performance, yielding these results with the JavaScript version of the RUSTBEL benchmark suite. We achieved these outcomes without utilizing any external libraries and maintaining full compatibility with JavaScript specifications. Our proof of concept prototype, built using JavaScript, securely manages the lifetimes of Rust data. This achievement stands for type systems beyond linear type systems, thereby facilitating future research on programming languages.

We explore Neutrinoless Double-Beta Decay within a higher-dimensional framework, with emphasis on the interplay between Majorana particles in the process. To achieve this, we characterize collider signatures of relevant neutral particles that can mediate the decay, including their mass spectra, mixing matrices, and couplings. A case study is made on a specific scenario involving a tri-Beta decay at colliders.

Traditional polar subcodes in low-density parity-check codes separate channels into good and bad categories by evaluating the channel capacity. The performance of polar subcodes is typically assessed using the belief propagation decoder, but its efficiency is dependent on the subcode's error vector, with some subcodes failing to perform well in simulations due to their limited error vectors. In contrast, some proposed subcodes, like successive cancellation polar subcodes, have superior error vectors, but their decoders are a modification of the traditional belief propagation decoder and lack direct comparisons with standard polar subcodes. The introduction of polar subcodes with cyclic nature in this paper leads to an average outcome in terms of error performance, and its corresponding decoder has been adapted from the traditional one with minimal alterations, thus enabling direct comparisons with standard polar subcodes.

The study of diffraction images involves a complex phase component which severely restricts the resolution capabilities of ground-based telescopes. Utilizing the phase information from the upper frequency range allows for the production of high-resolution diffraction images. The current method relies on the use of a low-resolution, phase reference image, acquired separately, to correct the diffraction image to be observed. This is accomplished via a Fourier transform and filtering operation. The present study aims to examine the influence of the phase reference image on the diffraction image. Consequently, the spatial frequency characteristics of the combined diffraction images were determined and analyzed. The results reveal that the phase reference image must be nearly free of distortions in its central low-resolution area in order for the combined diffraction images to be essentially free of distortions as well. The study further reveals that the phase reference image can introduce longitudinal distortions in the combined diffraction images, which are characterized and quantified. The phase variation along the axis of the diffraction image is found to be directly proportional to the angle of the tilted point, located in the center of the phase reference image. The study demonstrates that this proportionality constant is uniquely determined by the distance between the central points of the phase reference image and the diffraction image. The observed effects highlight the necessity for the phase reference image to be nearly circular in shape and for its central low-resolution area to be symmetrical in order to produce a diffraction image with high resolution. The fracture strength of solid crystals is examined and computed under minimal mechanical stress from their complex arrangement of atoms, using the Lennard-Jones potential. By combining elements of this model, the overall fracture strength is estimated as $\sigma_c = 3.63 \times 10^9$ Nm$^{-1}$ or approximately $\sigma_c = 371$ MPa with an uncertainty range of 104-437 MPa. These findings align with the experimentally measured values for amorphous silicon, which stand at $\sigma_c = (3.75\pm0.65) \times 10^8$ Nm$^{-1}$ or $\sigma_c = (36.7\pm6.5)$ MPa.

The relationship between SLEs and Gaussian free fields has been extensively researched. Specifically, the type of SLEs and its respective domain's field that matches, offers valuable insights into the field's correlation. This paper focuses on the connection between GFF and submartingales in Gorniy's class, which is linked with multiple SLEs that are driven by the eigenvalues of Gaussian matrix models. This involves the Schottky uniformization of domains, Gaussian unitary ensembles, and GOE's correlation kernel. GOE's correlation kernel is used to define simple conformal embeddings, resulting in the generation of submartingales in Gorniy's class. This is linked with SLE_{k,1) driven by the imaginary part of a Gaussian free field whose domain is the complement of a polynomially bounded simply connected domain in the complex plane. This specific connection with SLE_{k,1) offers the domain's correlation. This study further explores the observed connections between GOE's correlation kernel's radius, Gaussian free field's correlation, and the respective Gaussian free field's variance and the distance to the boundary of the domain of the half-plane.

In this research, we address the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional space, characterized by $d\geq3$ spatial dimensions and dimensions $x_1,...,x_d$. Given that the initial data, denoted as $u_0(x)$, is bounded and periodic across these dimensions, we derive an estimate that relates the maximum amplitude of the solution, denoted as $u(x, t)$, to its corresponding initial data. This estimate takes the form of a Strichartz inequality that involves time $t$, and is proven to be valid for all $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$, as well as for a specific range of exponents $\frac{1}{2}(d-2)+2^{-1}$.

The increasing reliance on quantum computing raises the concern for ensuring that these computations produce accurate results.  Unlike standard checks, which merely run the code multiple times and ensure the outcomes conform to statistical norms, a robust quantum verification mechanism would significantly boost public confidence in the technology.  The development of a reliable, compositionally-crafted verification procedure for quantum computations has been a long-standing goal in the field.  The creation of an interactive proof system verifying a quantum computation's correctness, by tackling the general quantum satisfiability problem, has been a key challenge since its 1998 inception.  The following paper introduces a groundbreaking verification algorithm for quantum computations, able to validate low-error quantum circuits in linear time and at a logarithmic depth.  The proposed method is an essential advancement towards the development of trusted, publicly-verifiable quantum auctions.  The study also outlines a quantum protocol for securely generating random numbers, resolved an oft-cited puzzle dating back to 1996, and has significant implications for future research into quantum computing.  The proposed algorithm is an essential component towards the development of widely-accepted, publicly-verifiable quantum computing systems.

A blockchain system enables secure interaction among entities through secure, decentralized transaction recording. In the context of Internet of Things (IoT), integrating blockchain systems proves challenging. The rising interest in applying blockchain technology to various IoT settings highlights the need for effective solutions. This study proposes a novel blockchain framework tailored for IoT settings, specifically including systems requiring swift, simultaneous processing of transactions by multiple nodes. The framework overcomes the "wait-for-validation" delay in blockchain transactions for IoT systems, allowing devices to promptly execute new functions after submitting and verifying new transactions. The suitability and effectiveness of the proposed framework are demonstrated through a practical application involving a food supply chain.

Cells are the basic units of life, exhibiting a wide range in shape and size.
To generate realistic cell models, we developed an innovative method that
uses function approximation to create a data-driven system for predicting cell
shapes. By training the function with comprehensive cell atlas data, we can
create a unique representation of different cell types. This approach allows
cells of the same type to maintain their inherent structural features and
characteristic scales, yielding a realistic representation. Additionally, 
our method preserves detailed morphological structures and features, and
enables the controlled synthesis of realistic cell models with variable sizes.

The ability to access and use printed documents independently is a crucial issue, 
particularly for those who struggle due to visual impairments, aged users, or users 
who are unfamiliar with the content. Our research highlights the requirements for an 
electronic system that enhances the navigation of printed documents, and we have 
created prototypes for both interactive displays and conversational interfaces, 
and shared them with users to gather feedback. The design process involved gathering 
input from users through interviews, surveys, and by observing how they interacted 
with our prototypes. The findings from these studies have shed light on the potential 
of navigational systems for print-impaired individuals and the tasks they need 
assistance with.

While BERT excels at handling long-range context by pretraining an aggressive auto-regressive model, it cannot consider previous words, making its pretraining inefficient. We have developed XLNet, a generalized pretraining model that balances the advantages of auto-regressive and generative methods. In the standard XLNet model, each token's sequence is conditioned on the prior tokens from one direction, while it conditions on the subsequent tokens from the opposite direction. To address the permutation autoregressive decoding limitation, XLNet introduces an innovative sampling strategy during pretraining. In addition, XLNet pretrains multiple times to fine-tune its language model. Notably, XLNet outperforms BERT on 20 out of 24 tested NLP tasks after fine-tuning on the GLUE benchmark. Furthermore, XLNet achieves state-of-the-art results on 19 tasks. Specifically, on the STS-B dataset, XLNet preformed better than the subsequent PERCEPTION model.

We have created synthetic, long-slitspectra using a Monte Carlo approach, simulating the effects of stellar activity on planets orbiting an active G-type dwarf star. This model includes data on photon flux from stars like the Sun and G-type dwarf star GJ 667 C, as well as data on its planetary atmospheres, generated using a radiative transfer model. We have analyzed this data using model-based analysis, a method of analysis developed to identify exoplanetary atmospheres. We compare the effectiveness of different high and low resolution spectrographs in detecting exoplanetary atmospheres, particularly in transit spectroscopy of active G-type dwarf stars. As expected, high-resolution spectrographs significantly improve our ability to identify the GJ 667 C e planet and its atmospheric features. We found that systems with active stars like GJ 667 C can be effectively studied with low-resolution spectrographs such as the Keck/NIRSpec, a forthcoming James Webb Space Telescope instrument. However, using low-resolution spectrographs may not be enough to improve our ability to identify exoplanetary atmospheres in systems with very active stars like HD 189733. Finally, we found that using low-resolution spectrographs with active star star spots may not significantly improve our ability to identify the planet's atmospheric features.

We will demonstrate the existence of a metric g, with constant negative curvature, that covers a compact Riemann surface S except for a set of singular points T, such that g's components are real analytic outside T, and g's norm |Ric|^2 remains bounded over T. This bounding result stems from a newly found estimate for the Laplacian of an arbitrary L^1 function on a compact Riemann surface. Furthermore, we can remove all singularities and still obtain a metric with minimal curvature, albeit one that would arise from a non-trivial process of deformation. This finding is achieved through first establishing a type of non-degeneracy for the 1-forms representing the fundamental class of a singular curve, and incorporating a variant of the Hormander theorem that handles exceptional sets defined by transcendental functions.

Research into the locomotion of creatures without limbs has traditionally been informed by studies of drag reduction techniques used in aquatic animals and aircraft designers. Expert swimmers, including geckos and centipedes, employ unique movements that are difficult to analyze using conventional rheological models. This difficulty arises from the complex interplay between Newtonian fluid dynamics and solid-liquid interactions that govern their motion. In this paper, we investigate the locomotion of a lightweight centipede species that exhibits remarkable speed when swimming through water, covering a distance equivalent to their body length in under three cycles. To better understand this phenomenon, we employed high-resolution digital recordings of the centipede's movement to measure its body oscillations and the resulting flow field. Our observations reveal that when this species swims through water, it generates localized zones of reduced pressure near the water's surface, despite displaying distinct differences from previously studied vertebrates. Our findings also indicate that the centipede's rapid movement is primarily driven by a unique combination of three-dimensional body vibrations and the revision of a previous model which suggested that rheological interactions could explain the observed rapid movement.

The widespread impact of tsunami waves generated by asteroid collisions with Earth can cause devastating damage, and their dispersion can be influenced by the ocean's characteristics, such as depth, topography, and dispersive effects. In particular, the friction that occurs as these massive waves travel inland can slow them down, while their dispersive effects can cause them to lose energy. In order to accurately model these tsunami waves, a high-resolution approach is necessary that can effectively simulate the complex interactions between the ocean and the resulting catastrophic events such as flooding, tidal waves, and massive loss of life. In this study, we are exploring a novel tsunami model based on the shallow water equations that incorporates an innovative spatial approach, such as triangular or quadrilateral meshes, which can simulate the intricate interactions between the ocean and the resulting disasters. By employing state-of-the-art algorithms, such as Kahan's method for preserving fractional parts and a vertex-centered, fully implicit temporal discretization, we are able to effectively model the complex dynamics of tsunami waves and their devastating effects on coastal communities. In addition, we are investigating the optimal numerical approach, such as the Jameson scalar dissipation model, which can effectively model the dispersive effects of tsunami waves and their interactions with the ocean's topography and depth. In a series of case studies, we are evaluating the effectiveness of our approach, such as simulations of tsunami waves generated by asteroid impacts in various ocean environments, which demonstrate the feasibility of our model and its potential to inform disaster preparedness and

Using new James Webb Space Telescope observations, researchers have found the first detailed views of certain galaxies that are too distant and faint to be seen by other telescopes. They have selected 57 such galaxies that are known to be massive and have high levels of dust, and are classed as star-forming galaxies. Analysis of these galaxies using a technique called H-alpha emission, which measures the interaction between the galaxy's star formation and gas, has revealed a range of information. By studying the galaxies based on their H-alpha to continuum ratios, researchers have discovered a link between the galaxies' infrared brightness and their levels of dust, and are able to separate different types of galaxies based on their star formation rates. Comparison of these new observations with data collected by other telescopes has shown a match between the galaxies' measured distances and their measured star formation rates, and are consistent with the galaxies' expected masses. However, some discrepancies were found in the galaxies' measured metal content, and are causing concerns about the accuracy of previous metal content measurements. Further analysis of these galaxies' properties is needed to fully understand their development.

This research focuses on constructing a seven-dimensional gravity model, incorporating terms with torsion and a torsional potential, which can be expressed using a specific frame formalism. We derive the model's equations of motion through variational principles and establish a decomposition of the three-form torsion, relating it to the Einstein-Hilbert action and a novel scalar field. Its effective Lagrangian is also determined and compared with General Relativity. We identify which constants are variable and which are invariant, and investigate how the torsional field influences the gravity field. Additionally, we recover General Relativity from the model and discover that the torsional field's presence prevents the occurrence of seven-dimensional black holes.

The channel is generated by the union of two horizontal lines: $y=a$ and $y=-a$, and contains all points between them. In this channel, horizontal lines of two types: $y=x+2a$ and $y=-x-2a$, are drawn, and all line segments between them are filled with blocks of two sizes: $2a$ and $2b$, and two weights: $w$ and $w'$, respectively. This result holds under a general condition: The absolute difference between the weights is finite, and one weight is greater than the square of the number of blocks, multiplied by a constant. We resolve a number theory problem by using our result on alternating sequences of blocked regions in a channel.

Two extreme flavors of the El Ni\~nO SSTA are characterized by their opposite seasonal precipitation effects in South America, Africa, and the Caribbean.  The strong La Niña SSTA, characterized by its strong and short-lived occurrence in 1950, results in extreme precipitation in these regions during the dry season. Conversely, the persistent and weak El Ni\~nO SSTA, observed in 1900, causes increased precipitation during the wet season. By analyzing SSTA time series from Sugiuhara-Kalnay-Fan standard from 1871 to 2010, the unique characteristics of these two SSTA flavors were identified and their impact on precipitation patterns analyzed. The study highlights the complexity and variability of two extreme flavors of the El Ni\~nO SSTA, emphasizing the necessity for a deeper understanding of these phenomena to improve precipitation forecasting and early warning systems.

The way solids grow is directly related to the type of particles making it up and how strongly these particles interact. By using X-ray scattering, we've found that during crystallization, the arrangement of particles is more complex and uncertain further away from the point of origin, which is characteristic of solids that grow irregularly. Conversely, in the initial stages of regular crystalline growth, the arrangement of particles is more uniform and predictable. Moreover, we've discovered that the level of irregularity in the arrangement of particles can serve as an indicator of the point at which regular crystalline growth begins. Furthermore, we've found that the shift from irregular to regular growth patterns occurs more quickly under higher pressure, which is pressurized using hydrothermal means. Lastly, we've found that the point at which regular crystalline growth begins varies depending on the type of particles and how hard the particles interact with each other under high pressure, which is pressurized using hydrothermal means.

In this context, a population model that takes into account the individual's age and behavioral influence is examined within an environment affected by pollution. Utilizing the Lyapunov asymptotic analysis, it has been demonstrated that the long-term population convergence trend is consistent across various environmental pollution levels. However, an increase in pollution levels can lead to a population that grows steadily, as opposed to a population that declines over time under lower pollution levels. Furthermore, environmental pollution gives rise to an intricate, non-monotonic population dynamics, characterized by a critical threshold beyond which the population enters a phase of exponential growth.

The previously investigated deduction systems for certain substructural logics have been re-evaluated for their decidability and complexity across multiple variations. The newly introduced hypersequent deductions were found to be comparable to the existing regular deductions in terms of handling both finite and infinite ordinals within these deduction systems. The analysis considered the various versions of these deduction systems, thereby providing a comprehensive framework for their analysis much like the one for regular deductions. The analysis of regular deductions suggested that they are either finite or semi-decidable across various parameters, whereas the analysis of the hypersequent deductions, being a more general version, allows for more flexibility in their analysis, thus enabling a more detailed examination that can also accommodate infinitary parameters. The analysis of the hypersequent deductions was then applied to determine the computational complexity of the deduction systems across various measures, while also confirming the previously established results concerning their complexity across these measures, thus providing a more detailed analysis compared to the existing results concerning regular deductions. The analysis of the hypersequent deductions was then applied to determine the computational complexity of the deduction systems across various measures, while also enabling a more detailed analysis of the various parameters involved, thus providing a more comprehensive framework for their analysis.

A hierarchical taxonomy is a collection of labeled categories that reflect their relative significance through a hierarchical structure, used for organizing concepts within a shared framework. Maintaining a balanced hierarchy is crucial to prevent overgrowing taxonomies, which can quickly become outdated and inaccurate. State-of-the-art taxonomy systems rely on hyberbolic embeddings, which visualize hierarchical data as points in a hyperbolic plane, but these models still struggle to manage taxonomy growth after grouping primary categories. Our new method, called HyperExpan, not only achieves but exceeds the performance of existing approaches in predicting taxonomy hierarchy, a task known as taxonomy completion, when evaluated on datasets within the fields of medicine and IT. The success of HyperExpan can be attributed to its ability to learn and represent hierarchical relationships within the taxonomy, and also to its innovative extension of hyperbolic representation learning for training on increasingly large data sets. The code and models used in this research are available for public use on the hyperexpansion-github page.

The accuracy of two widely used methods for calculating the interactions between molecular pairs in various conditions has been assessed. These methods, which model the effects of external electric fields, use a comprehensive set of data that includes complex calculations of molecular interactions. It was found that one of the methods, which accounts for the specific distribution of electrons in the molecules, provides a highly reliable prediction of the strength and direction of molecular interactions. In contrast, another method, which accounts for the specific distribution of electrons in the molecules, overestimates the strength of some interactions, while underestimating the strength of others. It was found that this method's inaccuracies are particularly pronounced in cases where the molecules have partial charges, or when the molecules are shaped in such a way that their surfaces intersect at sharp angles. Despite these challenges, it was found that this method provides a relatively good estimate of the effects of external electric fields on molecular interactions, and improves in accuracy when it accounts for a special type of interaction correction that accounts for the specific distribution of electrons in the molecules.

The fourth Industrial Revolution has significantly transformed manufacturing systems, introducing various data analytics applications to optimize complex processes like scheduling. Despite the advancements, many real-world applications still operate outside the boundaries of conventional deterministic or stochastic modelling frameworks, due to the presence of uncertain tasks. Characterized by a lack of precise data and varying levels of ambiguity, such tasks often go unaccounted for in current approaches. In this study, we aim to address this gap by proposing a novel methodology to identify and quantify uncertain tasks, leveraging knowledge from activity diagrams and fuzzy set theories. To demonstrate its efficacy, we evaluated our approach through a real-world case study from the packaging sector, comparing its results with existing stochastic scheduling models.

This study proposes a comprehensive framework for cyber-physical systems (CVPS) resilience by leveraging a standardized language to define resilience and flexible automated testing methods. First, a well-established logic is applied to create effective CVPS resilience requirements. These requirements serve as a model to assess system resilience, allowing for evaluation in various scenarios through automated simulations. Subsequently, a standardized language is used to define resilience strategies, which can be implemented and tested within the same framework. These tested strategies can be seamlessly integrated into the system, enabling the evaluation of their impact on CVPS resilience. Ultimately, a case study is presented to demonstrate the practical application and practical benefits of this framework.

Theoretical models suggest the presence of a widespread network of weakly-coupled particles, with theories such as narrow-resonance couplings to photons and the cosmic string network. Researchers propose using an extensive network of seismic sensors to detect these particles, as their collective operation could enable sensitive seismic data detection beyond current limits. The seismic background can be broken down into human-induced and natural components, with the latter dominated by weather and tidal influences. The seismic background peaks at frequencies below 1 Hz. Theoretical models imply that detected signals would correlate with sensor positions due to the anisotropic properties of the sensors and would exhibit temporal patterns linked to local weather, tidal forces, or other periodic factors. The seismic background can be further divided into local, regional, and global components based on distance, with the 1 Hz/ r velocity characteristic featuring a crossover at roughly 100 km distance from the source. The seismic background can be further divided into sub-components including earthquakes, waves generated by wind, and tidal forces. The theoretical models suggest that the presence of collective phenomena could result in reduced seismic noise below approximately 0.01 Hz. Theoretical models predict that detected signals would exhibit spatial correlations and temporal patterns linked to weather, tidal forces, or other periodic factors. We consider a semilinear diffusion equation defined on a complete, connected Riemannian manifold. By employing comparison principles, we establish the existence and estimates for solutions to the given equation. Specifically, we derive precise estimates for the solution's gradient and its evolution, assuming certain growth constraints on the reaction term. These estimates are particularly significant when applied to manifolds with dimension two or greater, as they facilitate the derivation of local asymptotic behavior and stability criteria for the solution.

By analyzing large radio source samples, researchers have discovered how galaxy properties change through evolution by studying integrated quantities such as brightness. Although unambiguous, this classification method has its limitations, as sources with higher flux densities have greater uncertainties in their radio spectra. To avoid such difficulties, researchers have turned towards statistical methods, specifically source stacking, which allows for a more indirect assessment of galaxy properties based on the distribution of integrated radio properties across different physical dimensions. We have gathered data on faint sources with flux densities less than 70 mJy through the Faint Radio Survey, and through source stacking, we have determined how galaxy properties change with physical dimensions such as velocity, distance, and angular size, also considering any potential resolution effects due to our survey limits. We have found that galaxies at lower velocities have fewer cold components, fewer hot jets, and higher black hole masses, also showing a decrease in kpc-scaled black hole masses with increasing distance. We have observed a correlation between source stacking and velocity or distance, also discovering that sources scaled by velocity or distance show similar characteristics to those observed in the z-RP relationship. We have observed a similar correlation between source angular size and jet temperature, also finding a linear relationship between source angular size and velocity or distance, also demonstrating how resolution effects due to our survey limits impact our findings.

Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are a well-established tool for evaluating a system's reliability due to their capacity to model complex behavioral dynamics and calculate the associated probability. HMMs are particularly beneficial for assessing security in distributed systems by quantifying the disclosure of sensitive data. HMMs can analyze the internal workings of a system using its observable input and output, enabling the calculation of a system's secrecy performance. Here, the HMM is further developed into an Abstract Hidden Markov Model (AbHMM) to broaden its scope and application. The AbHMM uses a generalized version of probabilistic transition functions, allowing it to be based on any probability monad, thereby increasing its versatility. The AbHMM finds significant applications in the context of quantitative information flow (QIF), particularly for evaluating a system's security level using measures like entropy. The AbHMM can be used to demonstrate a system's increased resilience when adopting mitigation strategies, such as the use of cryptographic methods, thereby showcasing its potential in the realm of QIF.

Building on the concept of consistency in physical systems, we establish a new framework for analyzing materials and their responses to various conditions. This approach, referred to as dynamic consistency, serves as a foundation for studying the statistical behavior of materials and their microscopic or macroscopic interactions. By examining thermal interactions, we identify consistent patterns of energy exchange and define a corresponding nonlocality measure. This measure enables us to quantify the degree of nonlocal effects in thermal interactions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that dynamic consistency and nonlocality are closely intertwined, as factors influencing one aspect can also impact the other. Additionally, we apply the concept of dynamic consistency to the study of fractal structures and their nonlocal characteristics.

We introduce a novel flexible framework for addressing the scattering of hadrons, 
where the fundamental components of hadrons are treated with minimal assumptions about their properties. 
The potential behavior of hadronic scattering amplitudes at unexplored regions is also considered. 
This proposed scattering phenomenology can accommodate various models such as Regge, QCD and Coulomb. 
In addition, we illustrate its practical applications in three contexts - establishing an absolute lower limit on the cross-section, 
distinguishing between two different regimes in scattering evolution, and accounting for a forward scattering spike. 
This phenomenology is versatile and can serve as a foundation for various models, such as those addressing the low-energy and high-energy regimes of hadronic scattering.

To comprehend how the Casimir effect impacts blackbody thermodynamics, we need to examine three fundamental principles: the generalized conditions of blackbody radiation, the quantum mechanical definition of entropy based on entanglement, and the momentum distribution of free electron gas influenced by the Casimir effect. This investigation will lead to a recognition of the differences in thermodynamic behavior attributed to the Casimir effect.

Location data serves a pivotal function in various social media platforms and services, yet users' willingness to share it is constrained by potential security risks. To facilitate location data sharing while safeguarding users' privacy, several anonymous location sharing services have been introduced, which hide individuals' actual locations behind one or more proxy locations to obscure their identities. Notwithstanding the implementation of these services, some concerns still persist, particularly the potential disclosure of an individual's movement patterns. To address this concern, our study proposes a scenario-based framework for measuring location privacy, which evaluates the privacy risks associated with an individual's movement trajectory when using proxy locations. This measurement is founded on a novel location privacy metric called Location Track Privacy (LTP), which is defined as the probability of different users sharing the same movement trajectory. By considering conditional priors for location data, our research demonstrates that LTP remains consistent despite variations in these parameters, which provides a crucial insight: location data privacy is unaffected by the choice of probability distributions as long as they share the same family. To validate the LTP metric, we conducted experiments on LTP for two-location and n-location scenarios and examined how LTP changes in relation to the distance between proxy locations, the number of possible locations, and the user's movement pattern. These experiments were performed using synthetic data as well as real location tracks obtained from a GPS-enabled device.

A highly complex 3D point cloud, characterized by its x, y, z and normal components, is efficiently represented using the Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) as a compact normal-based representation. This transformation, NDT-Transformer, is then trained to localize 3D objects in a scan-based approach, outperforming existing localized models such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) by achieving 1.8% higher localization accuracy on the benchmark Harvard-Bay area dataset. Additionally, our method has demonstrated significant scalability improvements by only increasing computation by 0.7% on medium hardware when dealing with an eight times larger dataset. This study's compact representation-based technique is highly adaptable and can be effectively utilized in real-world applications for 3D point cloud localization.

Connectivity mapping using resting-state fMRI remains a contentious issue despite widespread usage. This study delves into the statistical robustness of mapping across multiple brain regions. Using a vast dataset of 1,536 resting-state fMRI datasets obtained from 49 distinct brain regions, we examined a substantial number of connections, as well as the correlations and network metrics associated with these links. Our analysis reveals that the strength of connections varies greatly, with significant implications for mapping across various brain areas. Notably, we identify a subset of 24 regions that exhibit consistent connectivity metrics and show greater mapping reliability compared to the full set of 49 regions. Our findings have important practical and methodological implications, and highlight the importance of using multiple brain areas for mapping interactions, such as those observed in the cortico-cerebellar system.

This paper explores the principles of beeping networks, where nodes communicate via one-bit messages, and examines the naming challenge, where nodes must create unique names for local variables and messages to facilitate coordinated interaction. To address this issue, the paper introduces two key concepts: beeping channels and signal waves, allowing the analysis of beeping networks as a linear order similar to natural numbers. Building on this framework, the paper outlines a naming solution, and shows that the protocol developed achieves optimal results by conserving energy, thereby eliminating the need for initializations. Additionally, the paper presents a model checking-based formal verification of the protocol using Promela and Spin.

Recent advancements in NLP for code-mixed texts have gained considerable attention,
mainly centered on English-Spanish and English-Portuguese combinations. Most studies
involved using word-level categorical features. This research explores word-level
features with more effective methods to distinguish the contributing languages in code-mixed
text, focusing on the differences in morphology and syntax. A novel approach using
switching points for positional encoding in mixed text is presented, along with an alternative
feature representation that disregards standalone word categories. The results of experiments
on English Portugeuse text demonstrate the benefits of using word-level features without pre-segmentation. Additionally, the findings highlight the advantages of the proposed encoding technique over a widely used alternative in code-mixed text modeling.

The critical temperature of H$_{3}$S, approaching 250 GPa under pressure, shows a distinct variation in relation to the isotopic weighting of its hydrogen atoms. Depending on the specific energy level of H$_{3}$S as a function of pressure and energy, the isotopic effect may have an opposite effect, reducing its relevance at lower pressures but potentially amplifying it at higher pressures. Furthermore, calculations based on the phonon contribution alone underestimate the isotope effect at pressures exceeding 215 GPa due to the significant influence of a van Hove singularity near the Fermi level.

High-dimensional motion planning problems can be simplified through spatial reduction. This process involves transferring the complexity of the motion planning problem from a high-dimensional spatial environment to a lower-dimensional one, while maintaining the planning target. However, previous methods that utilize spatial reduction often fail to account for the dynamics of the environment, causing generated regions to be incomplete. This leads to planned low-dimensional paths not being realizable in the original high-dimensional space. In response, we introduce a new method of spatial restriction to motion planning that ensures generated spatial regions in low dimensions are accurate reflections of the high-dimensional planning constraints. This involves restricting the planner's domain of influence to specific, adaptable regions of influence. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a series of theoretical and practical tests spanning multiple planning tasks and scenarios.

A compact geometric representation known as a surfel map effectively captures the underlying structure of a scene. This study demonstrates that surfel maps can be employed for visual relocalization in 3D environments. To facilitate rapid detection of similar maps, a surfel-based query network is trained. To address the subsequent alignment challenge, a unique two-stage feature extraction model is utilized. To calculate the final orientation, a dual query network is implemented to find the optimal rotation for back-projecting, and a confidence score for localization is also obtained. Our proposed method outperforms existing techniques on several benchmark datasets and operates at a significantly faster rate. It can be accessed on the GitHub page at https://github.com/zju-openmv/3D_Surfel_LR.

In the context of the multiuser MIMO uplink, we examine the challenge of determining user choice, active user identification, and precoder design with the aim of maximizing the downlink sum-rate. We reconfigure this problem into an optimization task with the objective of finding the best subset of users and precoder that yield the highest sum-rate, while ensuring each user transmits at the minimum required rate. We develop two formulations for this optimization task and implement a technique that tackles these problems by constraining solutions to a specific format, while choosing the best subset based on the resulting optimization result. We test these designs with two different optimization tasks: one focused on sum-rate optimization and the other aimed at minimizing the gap between intended and achieved sum-rate. We combine the proposed techniques with an approximation method, Group LASSO, and find that they result in significant improvements in sum-rate compared to standard MIMO precoder designs.

Let $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ be a tropical curve. In this study, we establish the finiteness of the set of rational function semifields over $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ that yield isomorphic weight functions. Specifically, we demonstrate that the set of such rational function semifields over $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ with respect to a fixed weight function is finite if and, alternatively, the set of equivalence classes of weight functions that preserve isomorphism over $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ is finite. Furthermore, if $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ features insolated valuations at its irreducible components, we show that any rational function semifield over $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ belongs to a countable subset.

We consider the quantile function $Q_f(x)$ associated with a function $f$ whose distribution function $Q_f(x)$ increases with each component of a vector $x\in\mathbb{R}^k$. Given that $f$ has separated increments whose growth can be bounded, we prove that the difference $Q_{(n)}-Q_f$ of the empirical quantile function and the function $f$ itself converges uniformly to the process $N_{(n)/n}$ with functional norms that decrease to zero as $n\to\infty$. This generalizes a previous result for separable functions to those with separated increments.

The complex cohomology of the moduli space M_3 of genus three is investigated up to degree four, focusing on a specific Vassiliev invariant | |, which is revealed to be equivalent to the 32-dimensional cohomology class representing the moduli space's 32-dimensional cohomology class. It's also demonstrated that this Vassiliev invariant is isomorphic to 1 when integrated over M_3, but zero when integrated over M_2 for genus two. Furthermore, we analyze a specific cohomology class [x], which represents the pullback of a two-form supporting a one-form representing the Euler class of the universal tangent bundle T Q, found in M_3. This [x] is discovered to be a Vassiliev invariant of order three. In M_2, [x] is observed to be zero when compared to the total cohomology of the moduli space. We also explore an invariant, denoted as z, a specific complex number cohomology class in M_3, which is also a Vassiliev invariant of order three, along with the cohomology classes a and b in M_3. In M_2, z is observed to be a multiple of the second cohomology class representing the moduli space's Euler class.

At the crossroads of unusual superconductivity and complex hydride chemistry, 
materials based on $N$-type lanthanides and actinides offer captivating possibilities 
for exploring the relationship between charge order, antiferromagnetism, and high-$T_c$ 
superconductivity. Among these compounds, $LiFeAs$ stands out due to its unique 
properties: a unique $BCC$ structure; unique paramagnetic, nonmagnetic, and 
nematic-unnected states; and a $T_c$ remarkably close to its magnetic and 
orthorhombic instabilities. Notably, this site has asked whether the usual sequence 
of states applies: $P$ to $I$ to $NM$ to $SC$. In this work, we investigate the 
electric field response in $LiFeAs$ across its energy spectrum at a $T$ just above $T_c$. 
Notably, we discovered that the resonance at $\sim$ 15 meV correlates with phonons 
rather than with nematic fluctuations, as anticipated. Instead, we found that the 
low-energy spectral weight is dispersed across a broad frequency range rather 
than localized near the Fermi level. Moreover, we observed that the resilience of 
low-energy spectral weight to temperature is consistent with the chemical origin of 
the high-energy cutoff rather than with thermal fluctuations.

This research examines how the alignment of Type-II two Higgs doublet models relates to the predicted differences in the masses of the Higgs bosons and other subatomic particles, taking into account measurements from the Large Hadron Collider and the B meson system. The study shows that the Global Fit approach allows for a specific range of predicted particle mass differences to be validated, and based on this, it constrains the possible alignment of the two Higgs doublet model. The findings also suggest that future discoveries at the Large Hadron Collider and the proposed FCC-ee program can significantly reduce the possible range of predicted particle mass differences, and thus limit the possible range of parameters in the two Higgs doublet model.

We explore an optimized model for the self-assembly process of simple organisms composed of a basic central element and adaptable radial sections. Their adaptive structure allows a finite, pre-determined range of colors, denoted as 'catalysts'. This model is based on an optimized version of the classic chemotaxis model, in which the central element and catalysts interact through a modified Lennard-Jones potential, influencing the organism's movement and growth. A small subset of elite strategies, generated via an algorithm combining evolutionary techniques and a neural network, dictate the most effective color combinations and spatial arrangements for rapid attraction to a limited set of optimal catalysts or rigidly predefined colors. We analyze various strategy types, including fixed, random, and adaptive arrangements, the last of which adaptively evolves to counter a mutating environment. We also examine the impact of color limitation policies, such as a single-color, multi-color, and random limitation, and evaluate their efficacy in producing robust and efficient reduplicative structures with optimized arrangements.

We analyze the anomalies in chiral gauge theories with a gauge group SU(N) <th> SU(N+c) <th> SU(N+d), where the breaking of the gauge group is due to additional scalar fields in different representations. The effect of potential anomalies on these representations is studied, including cases where the representations have zero or non-zero tensor content. This investigation is performed within the context of the 't Hooft and Nieh-Yen anomalies in both two and four dimensions. In two dimensions, the model includes Wess-Zumino terms that contribute a quantizable Chern-Simons term, while in four dimensions, the 't Hooft and Nieh-Yen anomalies match those in three dimensions. In two dimensions, the loss of chiral invariance when the 't Hooft anomalies are not satisfied results in a bosonization constraint. In four dimensions, the loss of chiral invariance results in a non-favorable operator. In two dimensions, the loss of chiral invariance also results in a non-renormalizable operator, while in four dimensions, the loss of chiral invariance also results in a non-favorable operator.
