Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making it impractical for large datasets. A compact alternative is to represent categories using dummy variables, but choosing the optimal number of variables becomes a challenging high-dimensional missing hyperparameter for many models, including the Group Lasso. Although the Group Lasso is efficient in eliminating unnecessary variables, it cannot guarantee sparsity on the group level, which is essential for categorical data. A new method, Enhanced Group Lasso, addresses this issue by employing an additional penalty that controls the within-group redundancy, encouraging the Group Lasso to remove redundant variables within groups, thereby improving upon the traditional Lasso and Group Lasso approaches. Through simulations and real-world applications, the Enhanced Group Lasso has demonstrated superior performance in categorical data feature selection.

In recent years, the concept of multi-domain virtualization has emerged as an important aspect of embedded systems research. The growing need for real-time system security has led to the exploration of virtualization technologies in embedded systems. The increasing complexity of software systems has necessitated the partitioning of these systems into separate domains to enhance reliability, a trend further driven by the introduction of the Auto Sector 32 standard. The implementation of virtualization at the hardware level has become a widely adopted approach due to its inherent security and reliability benefits. The primary challenge in virtualization-based embedded systems is achieving timely interrupt handling and efficient memory allocation. This research aims to address this issue by developing a hypervisor, called T-Visor, which is capable of managing Linux-based guest operating systems on FPGA platforms. The T-Visor design is centered around providing a high guest detection rate, near-native execution speed, and adaptable memory management. The system comprises two guest operating systems, each running in its own domain, with the T-Visor hypervisor governing the execution environment. The design is grounded in a hierarchical architecture, where the T-Visor design aims to achieve a missed detection rate of less than 4% with an average interrupt latency of 200 microseconds. The effectiveness of the T-Visor design is validated through the evaluation of a benchmark suite, which revealed that the Linux guest system is capable of achieving 95% of its native execution speed on the same hardware platform.

Creating comprehensive 360-degree imagery necessitates merging discrete sections with overlapping fields of view. While existing algorithms focus on registration precision, they often generate multiple feasible solutions. To address this, we introduce a novel framework that utilizes context-aware cues, specifically gravity, to pinpoint minimal panormaic solutions. First, we evaluate existing orientation-determining methods, then devise a new approach that localizes vanishing points in each segment. By applying these orientation hints to each possible rotation, we filter potential registrations, prioritizing those closest to the most prevalent orientation, thereby reducing the candidate pool. Demonstrating its adaptability, our approach works with varied input resolutions and artificial noise levels, showcasing its efficacy in registering four or more images. For scenarios involving fewer images, our method provides a starting point for optimal solution discovery, outperforming existing methods, especially when considering realism-based metrics.

Building on the concept of chimeras first introduced in 2002, recent research has explored chimeras with uniformly distributed initial variability, resulting in a transition from secure attractors to complex, chaotic systems in a parameter space. This phenomenon was previously observed in systems with localized initial instability. The present study demonstrates the occurrence of this transition in systems without localized initial instability. Two distinct regimes emerge: a transition involving a stable chaos region separating secure attractors and a region featuring multiple, chaotic chimeras characterized by irregular, irregular spike patterns. For uniform initial variability, these chimeras exhibit stochastic spike patterns in a stable chaotic environment. The findings of this study underscore the intricate nature and high sensitivity to parameters of complex dynamic systems, as well as their diverse and often hidden behaviors.

We examine if deep policy search algorithms can learn robust controllers in uncertain environments. Currently, these algorithms optimize policies for simplified models but their effectiveness for complex real-world applications is uncertain. We adapt a probabilistic model-based algorithm that accounts for uncertainty in dynamic systems and allows for the optimization of controllers with limited information. We test this method in different scenarios and find that models with a certain level of uncertainty produce more resilient controllers than precise models. Also, the addition of noisy data enhances the resilience of these controllers compared to using noise-free data.

Building on concepts from Deligne's cohomology theories σ, we explore the structures of the resulting algebraic systems, with a focus on diagrams and their slices. By generalizing key notions from quantum field theories, such as higher-order algebras and coherence, we establish the fundamental principles governing these algebraic systems. In particular, we demonstrate the existence of an important subcategory in the theory of slices and show that it retains many of the original framework's fundamental properties. In addition, by extending the concept of coherence to the theory of slices, we gain further insights into the nature of these algebraic systems. In the process, we also obtain a new understanding of the trace concept in this context. In a separate approach, we examine the theory of slices in a monoidal form and explore the concept of modules within this framework. In a comprehensive conclusion, we address the broader implications of these findings for the theory of diagrams. By representing the underlying algebraic systems as diagrams, we reveal the simplicity and intuitive nature of these systems, while highlighting the significance of the structure formed by these algebraic systems in the context of the category of diagrams. In a separate development, we explore the cohomology theories in a multilayered framework and establish the important subcategory of linearly coherent systems. In a comprehensive conclusion, we conclude that the structure formed by the multilayered algebraic systems is well-coherent. In a final assessment, we conclude that the framework of the multilayer

Reflected quantum error correction codes, a subgroup of unitary quantum error correction codes, have unique properties that arise from their relationship with star tensor networks. This relationship implies the existence of a reflected structure within these codes, reflected at the quantum error level, affecting not only the physical state but also individual errors. This internal structure restricts the non-reflective quantum error correction code's ability to correct certain errors and imposes specific constraints on reflected codes that can correct the toughest non-reflective errors. In contrast to traditional quantum error correction codes, reflected codes have distinct characteristics when it comes to correcting noise that comes from multiple sources. Finally, we have found examples of reflected quantum error correction codes that can correct the toughest errors from one source but fail to correct simpler errors from another source.

Living organisms rely on patterns that persist over generations, such as the shape of a embryo's development or the characteristics of a species' morphology. These long-term patterns result from short-term processes, like molecular interactions or cellular interactions, that operate under stochastic conditions due to a dynamic environment and inherent random fluctuations. We investigate a general framework for pattern formation and persistence, especially in two-dimensional space, using statistical tools to measure pattern consistency. We focus on pattern transfer, a process that occurs when a pattern's features change location during cell division, and analyze how different mechanisms, such as pattern diffusion or pattern shielding, influence pattern stability. Our results demonstrate that the shape of a developing embryo is more resilient to disruption than we might expect, given the impact of random fluctuations, and we speculate about the potential role of pattern shielding in animal development.

We examine the three-dimensional generalized H\'{e}non model, specifically looking into the dynamics of the damped H\'{e}non model with a range of initial conditions. We find that this model's behavior is characterized by two types of attractors, namely fixed points and periodic orbits, subject to the constraints of the initial conditions. A further analysis is conducted on the model's eigenvalues to determine the stability of these attractors. Additionally, a new method is introduced to accurately plot the attractors using the Lyapunov spectrum, which aligns with existing numerical results.

The geometric interpretation of the Ricci idempotent endomorphism involves a crucial concept called gravitational holonomy. Furthermore, its essential characteristic is that it generates a trivial Stiefel frame. This distinct property allows us to identify only one possible gravitational holonomy in the given orthogonal frame. Consequently, we derive various formulas based on its uniqueness. These formulas ultimately lead to the derivation of the Einstein equation as a Ricci flow. This method provides a straightforward solution to the Ricci flow equation and also offers alternative implications for the graviton particle. The gravity field, characterized by the Ricci idempotent endomorphism, has a straightforward form when described in terms of the geodesic distance based on the minimal action of the gravitational holonomy. This distance-based action corresponds to a linear transformation that originates from the gravitational holonomy. The action of gravitational holonomy on Riemannian curvature endomorphism defines a gradient-like structure, which exhibits an inverse relationship with the Laplacian based on the gravity metric. This specific property enables an explicit formula for the gravitational holonomy based on the norm of Riemannian curvature endomorphism. The explicit formula involves an exponential function with argument derived from the gravity double integral. This explicit formula defines the gravity field, which can be expressed in terms of the geodesic distance based on the minimal action of the gravitational holonomy as a linear transformation that originates from the gravitational holonomy. The gravitational holonomy acts as a self-consistent, contractive

We focus on $\lambda$, a partition of $n$. Our discussions center around $h_i$, where $h_i$ represents the $i$-th hook length of the Young diagram associated with $\lambda$. Our analysis considers the set $\mathcal R_n^{\alpha \beta}$, comprising all partitions $\lambda$ of $n$ such that $h_i$ is divisible by $\alpha$ or $h_i$ is divisible by $\beta$. Our goal is to examine the distribution of the elements in this set, utilizing number-theoretic methods. These same methods can also be applied to the set $\mathcal R_n^{\gcd(\alpha, \beta)}$ or its modified counterparts. We derive the probability masses and provide limiting distributions for these sets. We also obtain the limiting distribution for the set $\mathcal R^3_n$. Our analysis extends to the joint distributions of the hook lengths. We utilize generating functions to study the set $\mathcal R^2_n$. Our findings are presented in a table form for the probability masses of the elements in the set $\mathcal R^1_n$.

Using the Larmor clock model, we investigate the correlation time $	au_c$ for spin fluctuations as the foundational element for establishing the quantum tunneling frequency $
u_t$ in a quantum system. Our argument is based on the notion that the uncertainty principle imposes a minimum duration $	au_c$ for spin fluctuation, and thus tunneling occurs at a frequency $
u_t \approx 1/	au_c$. By considering Larmor clock models with binary oscillators, we derive the relationship $	au_c = \hbar c_{\mathbf{B}}/2\omega_0$, where $c_{\mathbf{B}}$ represents the transverse Planck constant, $\omega_0$ indicates the Larmor frequency, and $\hbar$ denotes the Dirac constant. Our analysis demonstrates that the tunneling frequency $
u_t$ is directly related to the parameter $c_{\mathbf{B}}/\omega_0 = \hbar/\omega_0\hbar$, which is contingent upon the size of the binary oscillator units in a condensed matter framework. Our study indicates that the tunneling frequency $
u_t$ is inversely proportional to $\omega_0$ and the Heisenberg constant $\hbar$, and thus tunneling frequencies in condensed matter systems are generally very low due to the differences in $\omega_0$ and $\hbar$ compared to atomic and nuclear systems.

Leading twist distribution amplitudes for relativistic vector mesons, now studied in their nonrelativistic P-wave form, exhibit distinct leading behavior.  Calculations, both in the light-cone gauge with quarks and AdS/QCD, reveal the leading distribution amplitude as ${\cal N} z^2 \bar{z}$.  Notably, this result aligns with a leading twist ${\cal N} z^2$ P-wave function derived from the ket in the j-frame, whereas the leading distribution amplitude in the junction basis is ${\cal N} z \bar{z}$.  The kinetic term, ${\cal N} z \bar{z} \log z \bar{z}$, would dominate the asymptotic behavior.  The difference in the leading twist structure, either ${\cal N} z^2$ or ${\cal N} z \bar{z}$, depends on the twist order: the former applies to twist ${\cal N} 2$, while the latter applies to twists ${\cal N} 4$ and higher.  The kinetic twist-4 distribution amplitude, though containing the $z^2$ term, differs qualitatively by the presence of a twist-4 contribution proportional to $z \bar{z}$ as well.

A proposed set of nonlinear quantum operators can effectively model interactions within a Bose-Einstein condensate by accounting for the exchange of quanta between the condensate and quanta. This modeling begins with a modified Schrödinger equation that incorporates nonlinear terms, which gives rise to a set of nonlinear quantum operators. These operators correspond to specific transformations of the coordinate and momentum, mimicking the effects of a harmonic trap in a phase space. They enable the simulation of quasiparticle behavior within the condensate. It is demonstrated that as the number of quanta increases, the behavior of these quasiparticles adheres to the principles of quantum mechanics. Additionally, it is found that the presence of quanta in a mean-field trap can give rise to correlations similar to those seen in fourth-order interference patterns.

The extended BMS algebra $bmsm_{\pt}$, which encompasses BMS, DBI, and Lorentz generators with pt-independent cohomology, plays a crucial role in the study of soft gravi-photon theorems. Research has shown that pt-independent cohomology consists solely of the 2-dimensional N-extended Virasoro algebra, consisting of N copies of $u_{\pt}(2)$. We demonstrate that pt-dependent cohomology is far more complex, containing multiple distinct subalgebras for varying values of N. Notably, one such subalgebra matches a substructure within the DBI algebra for N equal to 3. We also reveal that N equal to 3 encompasses all pt-dependent cohomology elements, whereas this is not the case for N equal to 2.

Online learning without memory restriction can typically be performed by a single neural network, but when it comes to ensemble learning, the memory limitation remains a significant obstacle. Continual learning without memory in an ensemble setting has largely gone unexplored until now. This study initiates a exploration of this complex challenge, presenting a novel approach called the Neural Structure for Online Ensemble Continual Learning (NECL). NECL takes advantage of an online learning structure that utilizes a single neural network, while minimizing memory requirements by introducing set-point forgetting in the ensemble. We develop a continuous learning framework for the ensemble, and, to our knowledge, present the first online evaluation method without memory restrictions for the ensemble setting. NECL employs an interesting strategy where the diversity of the ensemble is deliberately decreased over time to facilitate learning within restricted memory conditions. We evaluate NECL on domain shift and class-increment learning, and observe that it allows the online learning structure to adapt and overcame the significant obstacle of decreasing diversity. Additionally, NECL's performance in online learning is shown to be comparable to existing state-of-the-art methods in continual learning.

In the context of hypercomplex, quaternionic and Hermitian manifolds, the notion of generalized forms is explored, allowing for the incorporation of metric information through an additional coefficient. Relationships between these generalized forms and Ricci flat four-forms are examined, particularly in relation to Hermitian manifolds. Four-metrics have been previously linked to hyper-Kahler structures on compact manifolds, with connections to twistor spaces and contact geometry in dimension three. This study recovers the existing definition of Ricci flat four-metrics in a more abstract framework and establishes analogous results for hypercomplex and quaternionic geometries, corresponding to the realification of hypercomplex and quaternionic structures.

In the wake of several recently constructed total permutation polynomials over finite fields with square orders, our focus shifts to analyzing total permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube orders through a detailed examination of permutation groups within the symmetric group $S_{q^3}$. Utilizing this approach, we establish various explicit examples of total permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube orders, with particular attention given to the cases involving small prime powers.

A recent study has revealed that approximately 24% of school-aged individuals, as well as 82% of pregnant women in Haiti, are infected with intestinal parasites. In order to effectively administer treatment programs, a rapid system is required for categorizing intestinal parasites, and this need has been exacerbated by the presence of multiple parasite species. In response, a collaborative effort has been undertaken to develop an automated parasite classification system using a single image, and this project has yielded promising results, laying the groundwork for the expansion of the system to support multiple images, and ultimately, the classification of parasites using mass spectrometry. Notably, the concept of Belief Networks has been utilized in machine learning for decades, and this study employs Deep Belief Networks to achieve high-quality Belief Networks quickly, and achieves impressive results on a dataset of 374 images comprising 11 categories. The introduction of additional data is anticipated to further enhance the system's performance.

This work introduces a novel approximation technique for a broad category of zero-sum-free stochastic differential investment and reinsurance models. It incorporates regime-switching models with both diffusive and jump components. The author's initial step is to reduce the model's non-zero-sum nature, followed by converting the model into a zero-sum zero-sum game involving two players. The resulting infinite-time direct dual Belopol'skov-Kalman-Brown solution is approximated in a finite-time direct primal form. The research demonstrates the approximation's accuracy, offering a practical method that can be easily implemented. The model's parameters, including its complexity, are influenceable factors. The method's efficacy is supported by numerical case studies which serve as practical examples, showing its practical value in reinsurance investment models.

This research presents a novel method for practical individual dual attitude (PIDA) control that combines proportional-integer-derivative filters with a dual simplex algorithm and genetic optimization, effectively controlling complex nonlinear systems with minimal flight time and increased efficiency. The proposed approach utilizes a dual simplex algorithm to solve a probabilistic optimization problem constrained by Gaussian functions, promoting smooth and stable dynamic model simulation. To enhance practical applicability, the proposed method is further augmented by incorporating genetic and anti-winding rules, significantly improving the robustness and performance of the control strategy, particularly in the presence of flight vehicle parameters uncertainty issues commonly encountered in real-world applications. The proposed technique demonstrates its effectiveness through detailed mathematical modeling and mathematical proof, as well as comprehensive flight tests conducted using a quadcopter.

Historically, pion-nucleon interactions at low energy have been difficult to study due to the high energies required to produce pions. Consequently, theoretical models have often prioritized high-energy interactions where pion production is more feasible. This focus led to significant breakthroughs in particle physics, earning Nobel Prizes in the process. However, the low-energy regime, characterized by small-mass mesons (e.g., meson-nucleon scattering below 300 MeV), remains less understood, with notable gaps in knowledge and no accompanying Nobel Prizes. Recent years have seen a shift in perspective, with increasing recognition of the importance of low-energy pion-nucleon interactions across a broad range of physics applications, including nuclear reactions, astrophysical processes (such as supernova explosions), and the study of associated radiation fields. This shift in perspective has given rise to various experimental methods aimed at quantitatively measuring low-energy pion-nucleon interactions. To date, a comprehensive description of low-energy pn interactions, encompassing processes such as the delta resonance and the pion-nucleon sigma term, remains an essential but unresolved goal in pion-nucleon interactions.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) experiment employs a silicon pixel detector to pinpoint the position of interaction points in high-energy proton collisions. As part of the upgraded CMS system, known as CMS Phase-1, the silicon pixel detector was enhanced with new readout chips that utilize the read-out front-end card (RFCC) system. For the initial data collection period, designers conducted an in-depth analysis to test the CMS pixel detector's functionality. This study aimed to evaluate the CMS pixel detector's performance and compare it with simulated data. To achieve this, the CMS pixel detector's pixel hit finding algorithm was developed and optimized. This work presents the initial results of the CMS pixel detector's functionality, as well as the effectiveness of its algorithms used in the first data collection period.

Detailed studies on the morphologies and environments of active galactic nuclei hosts are crucial in understanding their growth. Nevertheless, inspecting the hundreds of thousands of galaxies in the most recent wide field surveys becomes a significant challenge. We apply a machine learning technique, combining physical features with a random forest algorithm, to identify the structures of approximately one thousand one to three billion light year away active galaxies. The approach's reliability is verified through accurate two-dimensional modeling and good correspondence with expert judgments for 85% of galaxies, with the primary forms being both single super massive galaxies and smaller components. We then compared the galaxy structures with its star and gas amounts, finding no correlation between the former and environment, whereas the latter follows the galaxy's development. Moreover, we discovered a connection between the galaxy's mass and its central black hole's mass, adhering to the established Hubble Law.

A theoretical framework for characterizing the spatial structure of correlated events within the nucleus is developed. By modeling the nucleus using a one-body Wigner function, which accounts for zero-range forces, we investigate the impact of correlations on the nucleus's phase-space distribution. Our research demonstrates how the Q-value and binding energy distributions are influenced by correlations. Furthermore, we identify events with minimal spatial extension in the one-body phase space as a primary indicator of correlations. Our theoretical approach also enables the comparison of spatial structures in the one-body phase space and Wigner distribution of a nucleus with experimental data on momentum distributions and delocalization parameters obtained through scattering experiments. Our goal is to apply this framework to analyze events in the nucleus through momentum correlation functions observed in the momentum distribution of a nucleus, which can be accessed via a novel facility for high-precision scattering experiments.

This study addresses the co-domain equality issue in complex-valued deep learning by developing a corresponding complex conjugate constraint for complex-weight networks. Currently, the field employs the simple negative-complextity penalty to maintain co-domain equality but this approach has limitations. In contrast, the proposed constraint has numerous benefits including the maintenance of conjugate symmetry without extra penalties, the prevention of complex-dependent bias terms, and the facilitation of complex-weight initialization. Notably, the new constraint is flexible and can be applied to networks with or without complex-weight parameters as well as to those using real-weight hidden layers. Moreover, the proposed constraint can be combined with existing complex-depth networks with minimal modifications. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed constraint-based networks achieve lower F1-score variance, higher F1-score mean, and significant improvements in classification accuracy compared to the negative-complextity penalty method.

The non-linear QCD evolution equations ultimately lead to the saturation of parton fields when a sufficiently high density of partons is reached. Once gluon momentum becomes equal to a critical threshold set by the QCD coupling and gluon size, traditional linear equations fail. When gluon distribution surpasses this point, correlations among momentum states take over, preventing the linear divergence of gluons. Several key phenomena, such as the suppression of rapidity distribution at high energies and the emergence of geometrical scaling in various processes, can be attributed to the saturation of gluons. The application of such saturation concepts has also expanded into the study of heavy ion collisions, where observations of geometrical scaling in certain distributions have been reported in collisions involving lighter ions.

The study of stellar oscillations, particularly through the CoRoNet mission, offers several key advantages including the detection of extrasolar planets, rotation, and magnetic fields along with seismic signatures. However, the performance of the mission is hindered by the inclusion of low-metallicity stars, which result in a high degree amplitude dispersion, thus reducing the efficiency of the mission. In an effort to optimize the mission, the sources of amplitude dispersion need to be identified and addressed. In order to study a diverse range of low-metallicity stars, the study aims to identify and understand the causes of amplitude dispersion in seismic data, specifically through the use of a unique dataset consisting of 14 low-metallicity stars and 28 bright, high-mass counterparts. The study found significant differences in amplitude dispersion, with a sigma of 0.35 microHz^2 for long period stars, compared to 0.21 microHz^2, for shorter period stars. Furthermore, the study found a higher dispersion of 0.35 microHz^2 for the delta Suivers' wavelet transformed amplitudes, compared to 0.21 microHz^2 for the entire dataset. The study found that the major contributor to amplitude dispersion is magnetic field, with a correlation coefficient of approximately 80%. The study suggests the use of the Celletti-Lanzafame model in understanding and minimising the effects of magnetic field, particularly through the use of observational constraints. Evaluating how machine learning models perform in real-world contexts often involves assessing their performance across various scenarios, taking into account any uncertainties that may arise. Existing methods for making these evaluations are limited, and generally only apply to models with continuous output values, or to those that predict a single outcome. This research develops a novel approach for evaluating the performance of classification models that predict multiple possible outcomes. It is based on a statistical measure of variation, and our results show that this approach is more comprehensive and accurate in certain financial literacy applications.

A key distinction between human-made intelligence and intelligence born from complex systems remains largely unexplored in the field of quantum computing. To date, most quantum intelligence models have been limited in their capacity for systematic study due to their complex mathematical representations. The integration of Quantum Bayesian Networks (QBNs) in quantum cognitive science has paved the way for substantial advancements in understanding and assessing various forms of intelligence. The increasing accessibility of quantum computing devices, coupled with the emergence of new platforms such as the SQUID language and framework, is significantly accelerating the development and experimentation of quantum intelligence models. The versatility of quantum devices, capacity for parallel processing, and inherent ability for machine learning make them an ideal choice for studying intelligent behavior. The paper demonstrates the feasibility of studying quantum intelligence using the SQUID platform by reimagining well-known cognitive science experiments and evaluating quantum cognitive models. The experiments showcase the potential for quantum devices to develop their own decision-making protocols and the capacity for parallel processing in resolving complex moral dilemmas. The results highlight the significance of quantum devices in developing their own approaches to solving problems and the possibility of modeling human intelligence through its interaction with artificial systems. The experiments also emphasize the influence of quantum devices' unique properties, such as superposition and entanglement, on the development of intelligent behavior. The study further expands the quantum intelligence model landscape by introducing two innovative concepts: a multi-agent model for cooperation based on Drouet's, and a solo-agent model for moral decision-making rooted in T

This study explores warped product CR-submanifolds of almost contact manifold $(\bar M,\bar J,\bar g)$ for a specific category of submanifolds known as semi-inclined submanifolds. We find key constraints under which these warped product submanifolds can exist, given that the complex structure component is compatible with the almost Hermitian structure of the manifold. We also identify related conditions when the complex structure component is compatible with the metric, considering the pointwise classification of the warped product submanifolds.

The PALEOCCENE concept has the potential to detect nuclear recoil radiation with minimal energy using color center technology. This innovation could lead to the use of naturally occurring isotopes for direct recoil detection, bypassing the complexities of neutron sources and nucleonics. Although current technical limitations restrict the range of applicable isotopes, further research holds promise for expanding the palette.

Colloidal particles connected through attractive forces, represented as springs in certain systems, move in sync as they form complex structures that adhere to these attractive forces across varying distances. Studies have revealed that when particles experience a gradient in activity, their movement becomes restricted, giving rise to novel mechanical properties. In response, we investigate how colloidal particles linked by multiple springs evolve under these conditions. Through analytical and numerical studies, we find two equilibrium states. The first occurs when springs with similar mechanical properties align in response to the gradient, preserving the colloid's structural symmetry. The symmetry is lost in the second state, which is characterized by an organized arrangement of structures that vary in size. These findings can be observed visually, rather than through simulation, by manipulating a 2D colloid made of a mixture suspended in a gradient-producing liquid.

This research delves into the theoretical magnetic field dependence of energy spectra in the fractional quantum Hall effect, utilizing the Yang-Anzai-Lu multiple J-matrix scattering method. We extract spectral data and evaluate its relevance to observed experimental outcomes. Notably, varying the magnetic field at certain fractional values (1/3, 2/3) leads to notable changes in energy level sequences, causing some to reverse order. This phenomenon is closely related to a general rule governing the total energy spin in fractional quantum Hall systems. We also analyze SU(4) two-Particle holes data as a spin-projection approach into SU(4) symmetry.

Many outbreaks on networks can be modeled as a spreading process, which involves an agent assigning a value to a node; this value grows over time according to a non-linear process influenced by neighboring values. Systems are divided into categories based on final value assignments. This study utilizes a geometric approach to understand these systems, which are shown to cluster together within the phase space. Two distinct phenomena are explored: one, the separation of categories from one another; and two, the organization of categories within the space in a specific order. The former occurs when the system dynamics creates separate regions in phase space, which can be modeled using a simple equation; and the latter occurs when the system time-evolves to a secondary equilibrium state. This occurs in systems following certain growth patterns, such as linear or sublinear systems. Additionally, differences between systematic patterns versus random behavior are observed, which often result in greater organization in the latter. Finally, this study also explores the potential for an additional level of organization between categories, which occurs in systems following a specific growth pattern.

The reconstruction of cosmic microwave background (CMB) maps relies heavily on both the data itself and the statistical tools used to analyze it. One widely employed method, maximum likelihood estimation, often involves utilizing point sources, X'es, which can contaminate the data unless properly deconvolved. However, the statistical tools used in source recovery can introduce X'es of their own, stemming from the blurred angular bins and blurred Gaussian fluctuations. This paper examines the source recovery methods used in two CMB experiments, SMAC and BEEARS, to understand how to mitigate the introduction of X'es and maintain their absence in reconstructed maps. The investigation into X'es of their own began with a simple simulation-based approach and involved dissecting a single-source model to identify the source of the issue. The paper reveals that X'es of the data are significantly reduced once deconvolution occurs, but the statistical tools used in source recovery introduce new X'es. This problem can be alleviated by selecting an appropriate statistical function and incorporating cross-correlation information, which reduces the number and interactions of residual X'es. The sources of the issue were found to include anisotropic statistical functions and the inherent characteristics of blurred Gaussian fluctuations. This study provides a clearer understanding of X'es around Gaussian fluctuations and the source recovery process, and it offers valuable insights for improving the statistical tools used in reconstruction.

In goal-conditioned reinforcement learning tasks, agents are instructed to reach specific targets, and training data contains contextual information linking states to objectives. However, when training data is limited and multiple goals are available, the agent encounters referential ambiguity, making it challenging to interpret contextual objectives. To address this issue, the paper introduces a multi-agent training setup that involves training multiple agents simultaneously, each assigned to a distinct goal. As a result, the agent assigns low probability to objectives irrelevant to its current state, thus overcoming referential ambiguity and achieving better generalization. When applied to Hard-Phase Grid World tasks, the proposed method achieves significant improvements, surpassing previous multi-agent and single-agent baselines by 5-32 times. Additionally, the approach demonstrates strong generalization capabilities, reaching goals in novel, unseen states.

Quantum channel shadow maps effectively present numerous target channel properties
through easily accessible classical shadows, which can then serve as a valuable
reference for various quantum protocol applications. Beyond target properties,
these classical shadows also hold significant utility in their own right. Notably,
they constitute key components in state tomography and allow for effective
reconstruction of free quantum states. In addition, classical shadows serve as
a fundamental building block in channel tomography, where they play a crucial
role in reconstructing composite channels comprised of multiple independent
channels. In this study, we introduce the concept of shadow procedure tomography,
where we focus on reconstructing an arbitrary quantum channel solely based on the
respective classical shadows of multiple related channels. We establish theoretical
bounds illustrating the required number of these classical shadows needed to
reconstruct any quantum channel. Furthermore, we extend this concept to the
construction of composite channels and derive the minimum number of channels
required for their complete reconstruction. As an application, we demonstrate
how the necessary resources for quantum advantage in the fully indistinguishable
characterization of free states in the Repetition and Primality checking channels
can be calculated.

Given a planar body $B$, we define the set $A_B$ as the collection of second moments about an axis parallel to the body's diameter and the set $S_B$ as the collection of symmetric second moments about a diameter parallel to the body's diameter. This study investigates how to plan the most efficient route for a drone to take, with the aim of delivering items within a limited time frame while minimizing energy consumption. Various factors affecting the drone's energy intake are considered, including the type of payload, flight speed, air density, and the altitude at which the flight takes place. The three distinct factors that influence energy expenditure are then modelled using a suitable approximation technique and a suitable pathway planning algorithm is developed to determine the most efficient route for the drone to take, taking into account the time constraints of the application. The feasibility of the suggested algorithm has been evaluated through simulations that consider different variables such as the battery life of the drone, the time available to complete the delivery, the duration of the journey and the altitude at which the drone takes off. The results obtained from these simulations reveal that the suggested algorithm is able to reduce energy consumption by up to 51% in comparison to other more traditional route planning methods.

A computationally tractable renormalization group approach has been proposed for fermionic systems with Coulomb interactions, and applied to a particular case of bilayer graphite to predict a superconducting phase transition that occurs at a certain point. It's also been observed that this transition can be impacted by an external magnetic field. Additionally, this method has also identified other potential phase transitions and phase changes within the system that can occur. These predictions made using this method align with existing experimental and theoretical data and information. It also allows for a certain range of possible wave lengths for a particular type of wave that may cause a phase transition in the system to occur. These predictions can now be tested through experiments to confirm the potential for a superconducting phase transition in graphite.

Research on molecular spin systems has gained momentum in recent years, driven
by the distinct characteristics of spin interactions in molecules and the challenges
associated with realizing substantial interactions. Our study focuses on the Sc2TbN
molecular system embedded within a C80 fullerene cage, which we have successfully
created and characterized using a range of spectroscopic techniques including
magnetic resonance, infrared spectroscopy, thermogravimetry, scanning tunneling
microscopy, and ab initio calculations based on density functional theory. Our
findings reveal a symmetrical and stable molecular crystal lattice arrangement on
a nickel (111) surface at low temperatures. However, as the temperature decreases,
the molecular arrangement undergoes a significant change from a c(2x2) hexagonal
structure to a 2x2 square pattern, which is in line with simulations conducted using
thermal vibrations of surface atoms. Furthermore, our Sc2TbN molecular system
demonstrates antiferromagnetic properties with the terbium (Tb) ion at 1K, as verified
by the analysis of electron spin resonance spectra. Our research involves an accurate
simulation of a molecular system on a substrate and highlights the importance of
considering the influence of a substrate on the arrangement of spin systems.

The Internet of Things (IOT) is comprised of a diverse range of devices, including low-power, hardware-enumerated Security and Privacy (S\&P) capable devices. The existing guidelines provided by the IETF have proven insufficient in addressing the needs of these devices, primarily due to a lack of attention to performance and power consumption considerations. The proposed discussion will focus on developing best practices for the secure encryption methods such as AES and other similar algorithms, which are capable of providing adequate protection for sensitive data in low-power IOT devices.

The Ramsey sequence serves as an efficient tool for determining the frequencies of free atoms without employing the strengths of traditional Ramsey interferometry, as it leverages the direct examination of coherent superposition collapse to assess system resonances. Theoretical models predict that this method can generate accurate results at lower power levels and longer times than conventional Ramsey experiments. The implementation of a sequential Bayesian algorithm allows for maintaining a precise (on average) estimate of the resonance centre, as the model parameters are continuously updated based on experimental observations. The algorithm's integration into the Ramsey sequence protocol demonstrates that this method can accurately determine atomic frequencies, remaining resistant to prolonged external perturbations. The implementation of a sequential Bayesian algorithm provides a reliable solution for stable and efficient frequency measurements, as it serves to strengthen the overall protocol. Theoretical simulations confirm the viability of this approach and suggest that this method can accurately determine frequencies at lower power levels and longer times than conventional Ramsey experiments.
