The development of cellular communication systems requires accurate modeling of radio signal transmission. In this study, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to model the radio signal propagation environment. Based on downlinked data from 4G base stations, we trained the CNN to predict signal levels at untested locations. Compared to traditional path loss models, our CNN-based method yielded an average 5 dB enhancement in predicted signal level accuracy. Additionally, this technique allowed us to generate accurate predictions for both established and randomly generated test locations with minimal to no contextual information required.

A straightforward logic is proposed and its implications for achieving formal validation in temporal planning have been established. The logic is based on the Hennessy-Milner logic, which defines terms based on system behavior and does not concern themselves with specific system implementation details. By employing this logic, the behavior of temporal planners can be formally described, and its properties established using a widely accepted mathematical framework. Furthermore, the logic's capabilities allow us to ensure that the planning algorithm adheres to relevant time constraints. The logic's semantics was formally reviewed and proven using the interactive theorem prover Isabelle, in addition to modifying the input domain data into a compatible format. This effort marks the first instance of using a formal logic with well-established mathematical properties for temporal planning. As a result, the integrity of the temporal planner's design was formally validated. The logic's semantics and key properties were formally demonstrated, and the entire process behind the verification process were made accessible for review. The process of converting the input domain data into a compatible format, which is required for the verification process, was also carried out.

Power system expansion models, which are widely used, involve optimizing investments in generation, transmission, and storage infrastructure to meet anticipated load growth and flexibility requirements. The ability of these models to suggest suitable infrastructure investments relies heavily on defined parameters such as expected generation, flexibility requirements, and energy storage options. Studies on setting these parameters are sparse, and there is a lack of understanding about the impact of varying them on different power system emergence stages. This research proposes a framework to evaluate the robustness of power system models by assessing their ability to suggest equivalent investments across different scenarios. The framework involves defining a consistent investment pathway and then generating multiple power system models with varying parameters that match this pathway. The robustness of power system models was tested using case studies for eight countries with diverse power system development stages, covering three continents. The results indicate that power system models are highly sensitive to parameters like expected generation, flexibility requirements, and energy storage options, and relatively less sensitive to parameters like base-year load, network resistance, and base-year costs.

This study establishes the global existence of classical solutions for the 3D Vlasov-Poisson system and its generalized forms in bounded areas, under specified boundary conditions that include a homogeneous Dirichlet condition for the Poisson equation.

When conducting software maintenance, developers typically receive numerous, loosely related requests for change, described briefly by the developer and specified using natural language. In such cases, identifying the required changes is a challenging task, even for experienced developers, as it involves pinpointing relevant concepts within the project's source code. To assist developers in this task, a growing body of research focuses on automating concept location, while a recent study has surveyed developers about their needs and proposed a semi-automatic approach. Building on this work, our proposal STRICT uses natural language processing and information retrieval to quickly and accurately identify key concepts within a project's source code. To achieve this goal, STRICT first divides the code into distinct concepts based on a developer's request for change, as recorded in version control systems. Next, a search algorithm scours the project's source code for similar concepts. To validate STRICT's effectiveness, we have conducted a user study with eight participants, all experienced developers, which demonstrates that STRICT has met expected standards. Notably, a four-year code review revealed that our proposal sets a new, higher standard for successfully locating required changes.

Researchers have discovered a class of materials called "rheo-acoustic" gels by combining mechanical forces with acoustic waves for colloid particles. When exposed to certain conditions, these gels form quickly due to acoustic repulsion, allowing for the study of their internal structure and movement through ultrasonic waves. Studies have shown that these gels have solid-like properties under static conditions, yet they can be broken down by acoustic forces, transforming into fluid-like states that can flow freely. Moreover, acoustic waves can repair and rebuild such gels when they're deformed, without needing heat treatment. What's more, researchers found that ultrasonic waves can improve the gel's ability to flow by reducing its viscosity, all while maintaining its unique structure. Notably, these improvements last beyond the duration of the acoustic waves. Through further analysis, researchers found that local rearrangements and changes in the material's structure occur rapidly in response to acoustic waves, leading to long-lasting effects on the gel's rheological properties. This breakthrough offers a new method to transform and improve the structure and flow of materials within living and non-living systems.

The Collatz Conjecture is a mathematical hypothesis concerning a specific function introduced by John Horton Conway as the "3x+1" problem. It states that its values evolve according to the following rules: if the current number is even, it is halved; if it's odd, it is multiplied by 3 and then added to a half. The Collatz Conjecture asserts that regardless of the initial value, successive applications of this function leads to an infinite sequence whose terms alternate between even and odd numbers, eventually reaching 1. While extensive research has been conducted, no formal proof or counterexample has been found since its initial presentation in 1930, with many renowned mathematicians attempting to resolve the issue. Given its relative simplicity, the problem has been largely accessible to beginners; as a result, numerous mathematicians including professional academics and laypeople have explored and explored the issue. We will examine a particular case that seems straightforward.

Incorporating mathematics into science, technology, engineering, and mathematics fields has become a difficult task due to the varied ways of expressing mathematical concepts. Despite significant advancements in natural language processing and access to vast amounts of digital data, accurately understanding mathematical terms remains a significant challenge. This study focuses on a particular problem within academic document analysis - classifying importance by relevance - which entails identifying the significance of individual words within discipline-specific contexts. To address this problem, we analyzed a particular discipline-specific dataset and examined the limitations of relying solely on token-level dependencies. Instead, we propose considering mathematics as an integral language and developed a model that identifies and links crucial mathematical entities within a document. By leveraging both inter-entity and intra-entity relationships, our model has the potential to assign more comprehensive significance scores. Building upon this approach, we explored the effectiveness of entity-based significance scores in relevance classification and found that this method significantly outperformed traditional token-based models.

The process of finding a suitable match, or a stable pairing, involves two groups, typically representing suitors and service providers, with members from one group seeking matches from the other. Each individual has a hierarchy of preferences, or ranking, for potential matches. Given these preferences, Suitor j is interested in finding the most preferable matches from the list of Service Provider i's, or more broadly, Proposal pairs (i, j). Given these pairings, each pair is asked if they would like to commit to a match, with commitment being voluntary and safe from manipulation. We are looking for a rule that determines which pairings can safely commit without threatening matching stability. We discovered that the traditional stable matching approach can be seen as a specific case where the hierarchy of preferences is maximally extensive. We explored the properties of the proposed rule and found that there are situations where the hierarchy of preferences is not complete, thus allowing for a more selective approach in matching suitability. We found this rule to be fair and non-discriminatory. We also discovered that the proposed rule has a straightforward and easy-to-implement approach compared to other, more complex algorithms used in matching theory. We also demonstrated that the proposed rule prioritizes matches of higher value and is fair to un matched individuals, while also determining the suitability of matches in a progressive and uniform manner. Current assessment metrics for summarization models are mainly targeted at 
detecting biased, sensationalized, and overly lengthy summaries. However, 
models optimized by these metrics often generate low-quality summaries with 
exaggerated and biased content. To address this issue, we present SummScore, a 
more comprehensive metric that aims to improve summary quality in multiple 
aspects. Based on the BERT model's advanced language representations, SummScore 
uses a Cross-Encoder architecture to assess summary quality by comparing the 
relevance and redundancy between the original text and the summary. During 
training, SummScore is marked by high correlation with human assessments, 
outperforming existing assessment metrics. Moreover, our research demonstrates 
that learning to work with SummScore can enhance the performance of summarization models, resulting in better scores on various assessment metrics in a 
downstream task. These improvements are especially noticeable when combining SummScore 
with rewards related to summary length.

In various fields such as compressed sensing, quantum information, and data recovery techniques, the goal is often to obtain accurate signal representation through measurements and subsequent processing. Traditional theories typically emphasize the importance of in-depth analysis and precise conditions for meeting this objective. This study, however, takes a contrasting approach where it is demonstrated that under a broad set of mild conditions, the signals can be quickly restored from a quadratic model even with random measurements, a transition that occurs when signal sparsity exceeds a critical threshold which aligns with established guidelines in conventional theories. This recovery is facilitated through a convex optimization program, and a convex order-theorem provides the basis for this outcome. Notably, the proposed quadratic model encompasses a broad range of signals, including traditional sparse types, and the study provides an estimation of the necessary signal sparsity for accurate recovery. This estimation is performance-optimal and based on the worst-case scenario in a prescribed convex gauge function, and it generalizes well to linear models where signals are defined by gauge functions. This study also provides additional insights into the performance of linear models. Furthermore, the study offers a dual perspective on the issue, resulting in new findings in convex geometry that can be useful in other contexts.

The primary goal of 3D object detection in autonomous driving involves locating and classifying objects in a scene. Current camera-based approaches can identify some non-LiDAR objects, like trees, which are crucial for scene completion, but struggle with LiDAR-only methods, which may fail to detect post-sign posts. In contrast, camera and LiDAR data together offer significant improvements in detection quality and coverage, making fusion a highly sought-after solution for 3D object detection. However, existing fusion architectures often rely on expensive feature matching processes, unreliable beam-forming methods, or simple feature copying, which come with their own drawbacks, such as the risk of feature distortion and loss during the fusion phase. To address these issues, we introduce BEVFusion, the first LiDAR-camera fusion framework that operates directly in the BEV domain. By incorporating a simple feature fusion module, where features are fused based on semantic relevance rather than spatial proximity, and utilizing a shared encoder for LiDAR and camera features, we avoid the need for expensive feature matching processes. Our framework also employs a novel beam-forming method with an attention module, which enhances feature fusion by detecting overlapping regions with high attentional scores. As a result, we achieve superior 3D object detection performance with better mAP and average detection quality on several benchmark datasets. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com-soonho-park/BEVFusion.

In the context of magnetohydrodynamics, thermal disturbance in solar flares belongs to the dissipation range of fluid turbulence. Moreover, the Rees mechanism that produces acoustic waves via the reflection of thermal disturbance at the photosphere can be confined to this range. Utilizing the concepts of the nonlinear theory of the dissipation range developed by Cox and Kichatinov (2000), we have developed a mathematical model describing the temporal evolution of thermal disturbance. The model relies on the nonlinear interaction with the background stratification of the atmosphere. The model's spectral density decreases as the wavenumber increases and a characteristic frequency decreases with wavenumber, approximately proportional to the square root of the wavenumber. These properties align with the characteristics observed in data. The model shows that the spectral density exhibits a peak at an optimal wavenumber and decays towards higher wavenumbers. The optimal wavenumber changes with time, increasing as the 3/4 power of the square root of time. The model's frequency characteristics can be explained by the slow increase of the spectral density, while the optimal wavenumber shifts towards higher values due to the decay of the spectral density. The model's findings align with the characteristics observed in data.

The behavior of light as it interacts with a heated medium is influenced by thermal distortions induced by the light itself. In certain media, the presence of heat-induced gradients gives rise to refractive index changes that can produce interferences, resulting in the observation of dark spots or rings in the output of the medium. The pattern that emerges is a direct consequence of the interplay between thermal effects and the laser itself. In a study focused on the behavior of laser light as it passes through a heated medium, we have made detailed calculations regarding its spatial and temporal evolution. The model developed accurately accounts for energy absorption by the medium, the resulting temperature distribution, and the effects of absorption and scattering of the laser light as it travels through the medium. The effects of heat-induced refractive index changes on the laser light have been calculated, and the model predicts the dark spots or rings that will form in the output of the medium. In cases where the laser light undergoes significant scattering, the model includes a representation of the energy distribution across different paths. The model predicts a four-leaf pattern in the output of the medium and the splitting of the dark spot into two, depending on the sign of the thermal refraction. The model has been applied to various parameters and the results compared with existing experimental data. The model developed accurately accounts for energy absorption and scattering, and the effects of heat-induced refractive index changes on the laser light.

achieving consensus among experts, leading to varied interpretations of a single 
set of results. This research aims to a) explore and document the process of 
concluding b) within this study, a set of design decisions was made regarding 
user-defined data fields for ticket tracking systems and to reach a conclusion, 
design stakeholders were asked to provide their opinions, which were then

The rise of Smart Cities, along with other communities, now generate vast amounts of streaming data from diverse sources, including IoT devices, network traffic, and online content. These data are invaluable for decision-making within the metaverse and traditional societies, facilitating enhanced city services, optimization, and decision-making through urban informatics. However, integrating real-time data from various sources poses significant IT challenges, including data extraction, validation, storage, analysis, and visualization. For instance, transportation systems need to optimize traffic flow, while healthcare aims to monitor patient well-being and security seeks to identify potential threats. While Big Data platforms excel at historical analysis, stream processing capabilities are underutilized, with solutions often developing in isolation. This paper presents H-STREAM, a versatile analytics pipeline architecture for stream processing and data history analysis, incorporating modularity, flexibility, and adaptability. It employs a unified processing technique for both streaming and historical data, addressing the limitations of current solutions. H-STREAM's design enables efficient resource allocation and data integration, along with a plug-and-play pipeline architecture for various processing modules and data sources. It allows users to specify and customize data analysis and visualization workflows through a high-level configuration language. These pipelines can be executed and managed by the H-STREAM engine, which ensures data consistency and ensures that all involved processing modules are properly configured. The paper showcases H-STREAM's capabilities by demonstrating its application in various use cases, including smart cities, healthcare, and cyber security, highlighting its benefits in data

The production of single color-singlet particles at the LHC is an intriguing topic 
that hasn't been extensively explored yet, despite the significant role it could play 
in uncovering new physics. To further understand how this process might work at 
medium energy levels, we examine the production of the top and bottom partners at 
 energies slightly below the threshold for their decay into standard model particles. 
Using an established model of particle dynamics called Effective Field Theory, we 
calculate key aspects of the interaction between these partners and the proton. 
Given that we don't have any concrete information about these particles, we use a 
theoretical model to simulate various properties of the top and bottom partners. 
Ultimately, our analysis suggests that experiments conducted at the LHC using 
proton-proton collisions at specific energy levels might be able to detect these 
particles.

SPARQL translation involves converting SPARQL queries and RDF datasets into equivalent queries, a complex task requiring in-depth understanding of both. Conventional methods often focus on translating SPARQL queries, but overlook the importance of also adapting the underlying RDF dataset. This paper proposes a groundbreaking approach to SPARQL translation by simultaneously translating both queries and RDF datasets, drawing on the concept of multi-task learning. An innovative technique is presented for identifying and mapping central concepts within RDF datasets, analogous to word copying in neural machine translation. The proposed method also includes controls to prevent incorrect predictions. Experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods.

This work introduces a straightforward yet effective alternative to traditional citation-based metrics for evaluating researcher productivity and the quality of a particular venue in publishing high-quality research. By substituting citations with a more direct statistic – the number of significant publications recognized with an award or prize in the field, we demonstrate that a significant correlation exists between this simpler metric and the ultimate impact of those publications as measured by the number of subsequent citations they receive. Furthermore, through an examination of varying fields of study, we establish that such awards serve not only as a reliable indicator of a publication's overall impact but also, more critically, its long-term relevance and continued influence over time. Additionally, by showing that award-based metrics capture a distinct aspect of a publication's ultimate impact that is not reflected by citations alone, we highlight the inherent limitations of citation analysis in assessing a publication's ultimate sustained influence. In an effort to foster greater transparency and accountability in the field, we develop an accessible, automated system for collecting and monitoring such awards and influence metrics, which can be configured and tailored to various research areas and their distinct conventions.

The growing presence of neural networks (NN) in control systems poses new challenges, particularly with regards to ensuring the reliability of NN-based controllers. This work aims to build on existing research validating NN and will focus on exploring new areas, such as integrating validation for control systems, a topic largely unexplored.

The process of clustering, or functorial hierarchical clustering, enables the creation of a commutative diagram where each node represents a space representing sets of points within a hierarchy, or input dimensions, and represents a functor that establishes a relationship of equivalence between the space and a reference space. This equivalence is achieved through a metric or semi-metric approach. The purpose of this method is to facilitate interpretation of clustering results by providing a meaningful framework for comparison, and addressing challenges associated with traditional clustering approaches that rely on ad-hoc decisions. Furthermore, functorial hierarchical clustering offers the ability to interpret results using theoretical characteristics of the cluseters, and maintains a level of generality to allow the application of various metrics and semi-metrics.

The tensor completion problem seeks to recover missing data in a tensor given observed components. This problem has far-reaching applications and is well-suited for addressing missing or corrupted information on streaming platforms due to its high data efficiency and favorable streaming properties. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces the patch tracking-based streaming tensor loop completion model (STLC), which is a novel approach to recovering tensor data in a real-time streaming environment. The proposed model incorporates an innovative anisotropic flow process that is more resistant to noise than its isotropic counterpart. The anisotropic flow process is based on the geometrically-inspired direction of incomplete tensor components, making it more effective than isotropic approaches. The model's performance was tested using the CMU face tensor dataset, and the results demonstrate that STLC outperforms existing tensor completion models both numerically and visually. The proposed model is also adaptable for streaming tensor completion, where it achieves accurate recovery results even with a 99.9% data loss rate without compromising real-time processing capabilities. Notably, this model can be executed in a parallel processing environment, such as CUDA, at a remarkably fast rate, completing the inference process in less than 0.1 milliseconds with a high throughput of 85.67 frames per second.

It is demonstrated that for a broad category of Weyl groups G, associated Nichols algebras are classified under the sole condition that their root lattices have an even Coxeter graph. This generalization applies to Weyl groups of all ranks, excluding those of Lie type $E_6$. The study relies heavily on the findings from Part I, in addition to the classification of infinite order Nichols algebras and the extension of Brauer formula applicability to Weyl groups.

This paper presents an in-depth examination of simulated wave turbulence driven by a mild energy flux. The analysis confirms the presence of a distinct frequency power-law spectrum with an exponent of -7/3 over a broad wavenumber range, along with other expected frequency patterns related to energy injection and decay. Notably, this result aligns with recent direct and narrowband lidar measurements from the North Sea. Additionally, the study reveals a frequency shift in the negative frequency skewness as it diverges from its equilibrium value, implying increased tailweight in the energy distribution. Further investigation is recommended to determine the physical implications of this phenomenon.

For a given graph $G = (V, E, W)$ with weight function $w$, we aim to find the maximum-weight independent set (MWIS) that satisfies specific weight conditions. Traditional algorithms for identifying MWIS on weighted graphs are plagued by suboptimal efficiency, leading to a need for iterative enhancement via repeated calculations of a normalized graph, where vertex weights are adjusted proportionally to the number of adjacent vertices. However, these methods are hindered by a complexity increase of at least quadratic with each iteration. We propose a novel approach that leverages set transformation and independent set properties to identify a normalized graph through a single, efficient process, thereby significantly improving computational complexity to a linear process. We demonstrate its applicability across various weight conditions, and showcase its adaptability to encompass additional constraints, such as those based on graph radius.

This research focuses on exploring the thermodynamic properties of electrically controlled graphene monolayer. Our investigation utilizes the Landau-Ginzburg theory in combination with the mean-field approximation to analyze the model, which has been established based on the electron-sublattice-phonon interaction concept. We have investigated the impact of various external factors, such as magnetic and electric fields, on the system's behavior. Our study reveals that the system's phase structure depends on chemical potential, magnetic field intensity, and external periodic perturbations. We have further examined the thermodynamic properties of the system under these influences and found that its behavior is characterized by distinct phase transitions at specific chemical potential and external field intensities.

The system CR Draconis, consisting of two closely related flare stars in the constellation of Draco, was studied over a period of nearly five years using a 30-m radio telescope. Observations indicated that in 85% of cases, CR Dra proper moved across the sky at a rate of $40\pm5$ mas per year in a generally northerly direction, with annual increases in its proper motion accounting for by $80\%$ of this movement. It was discovered that CR Dra e, the less luminous component, shows persistent low-frequency radio emission, possibly the result of an electron-cyclotron maser process. A unique radio emission regime was found in CR Dra, characterized by its dependence on time, speed, and other factors, with features such as sharp rises and declines, complex patterns and relatively low frequencies. It was also suggested that in order for radio emissions to occur more frequently, the two stars in the system CR Dra must be in close proximity to each other, with an estimated separation distance of less than $10,000$ km.

The incorporation of user-generated avatars in online communities is becoming increasingly common, with potential applications in social media, online gaming, and virtual meetings. However, current visual representations of avatars are static and limit users' ability to understand each other's movements and behaviors. To address this issue, we developed Articulated Neural Representation (ANR), a pioneering technique that enables the 3D visualization of fully articulated avatars from a single two-dimensional image. Our approach differs from existing methods by automatically defining and aligning key 3D features without human intervention. Notably, ANR can generate lifelike 3D representations from images of individuals in various poses, without the need for benchmark datasets or precise calculations. Our results demonstrate that ANR can effectively reconstruct 3D models from a single image, both accurately and efficiently. Additionally, we applied ANR to a dataset of social media images to allow virtual explorations of user movements and behaviors. To facilitate research, we publicly released our source code, models, and related data.

There are significant variations in how effectively humans and machines cope with severe alterations to visual data. While machines are hindered in their ability to process such changes, humans exhibit more resilience. This dissimilarity arises from distinct weaknesses. Machine weaknesses stem from inadequate representation capabilities, whereas human adaptability stems from efficient information processing. This study introduces a novel method for evaluating the severity of image transformations relative to each other, incorporating both human and machine performance. We investigate whether the proposed metric, designed to capture both representation and transformation aspects, can distinguish between different types of image changes. Additionally, we explore whether the distances between different transformations, as measured by human judgment, are in line with those evaluated by machine performance.

The relationship between the Askey-Wilson matrix and the Poisson transform of CS theory has led to a finding. A unitary representation of the braid group exists, defined by the AW matrix, and the eigenvalues of the corresponding matrix are unitary transformations of the CS invariants for links. Additionally, the spectral decomposition of the CS invariants for links can be expressed using the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the AW matrix.

Our study involves the use of a cluster quantum Monte Carlo algorithm in an investigation of the two-dimensional Ca$_{2}$Mg$_{2}$(SO$_{4})$_{3}$($ClO$_{4})$_{2}$ antiferromagnet. This system consists of a strongly coupled two-dimensional triangular lattice at intermediate temperatures and a weakly coupled network of ferromagnetic bonds at lower temperatures. At high temperatures, our results show that the lattice exhibits short-range entropy similar to that of the two-dimensional Heisenberg model. As the frustration increases, our findings show a transition from dominantly hexagonal clusters to pentagonal ones. Further investigation revealed that the hexagonal cluster model can explain the observed transitions between different domain walls within the system at lower temperatures, whereas the formation of pentagonal clusters cannot be accounted for through existing theoretical frameworks. A proposed new model involving a hexagonal-ferromagnetic penta unit is shown to effectively describe the evolution of magnetic correlations in the system at low temperatures. This includes the appearance of ferromagnetic bonds within the unit and the associated magnetic waves spreading across the hexagonal penta unit. At the lowest temperatures, our results show a first-order transition between the high-temperature hexagonal penta phase and the proposed new phase, where magnetic waves are shown to be in-phase. These findings highlight the magnetic waves as a potential new signature of the existence of the magnetic solenoid in the model, which consists of the high-temperature

Pre-trained language models can be adapted for zero-shot learning tasks using few-shot learning techniques. Our research focuses on the'meta-learning' approach, developing a method to prepare models for a variety of tasks without explicit training. We test this method on the Hateful Memes Challenge, a dataset assembly consisting of several social media platforms' text classification tasks. Our model achieves 74.0% accuracy, surpassing the current state-of-the-art of 67.2% achieved by the competition winners. We also introduce the concept of 'Dataset Assemblies' - a means to categorize public datasets based on similar characteristics, and 'Prompt Assemblies' - a way to group prompts according to their similarities. We map the Hateful Memes Challenge dataset assembly to its reduced form, consisting of three sub-datasets corresponding to Dataset Assemblies, and apply our method to each. Our model's performance shows significant variability depending on the sub-datasets, indicating the importance of taking into account the characteristics of a dataset assembly when evaluating its results. Additionally, we observe the 'Prompt Assembly Effect' - a noticeable improvement in the model's performance when using prompts from a specific group, yielding an average 6% gain in accuracy. Our findings also highlight the 'Dataset Assembly Curse', where the distribution of labels within an assembly may conflict with that of another, causing inconsistencies in the model's predictions and resulting in lower performance.

Significant insights into certain theoretical aspects of particle physics can be derived from observations of key phase transitions, including the electroweak baryogenesis and cosmic gravitational waves. Focusing on a specific particle theory known as the $Z_3$-invariant NMSSM, this study extensively examined how various theoretical models influence predicted patterns of high-energy particle behavior, with emphasis on the naturalness of high-scale particle interactions and the naturalness of dark matter within these models. Additionally, this investigation considered the relationship between the models and predicted high-energy particle collisions at future particle physics experiments. The results of these analyses indicate that sufficient conditions for natural electroweak phase transitions and dark matter stability can be satisfied, with the latter occurring at a temperature of around 80 GeV. Such an event would generate a significant first-order phase transition, producing a significant impact on the universe's baryon density and potentially detectable through cosmic observations of gravitational waves. The predicted spectrum of high-energy particle behavior within the models was found to be characterized by heavy scalar bosons and gluon bosons, with a significant difference in mass between the two. The studies also suggest that future particle collision experiments could potentially observe heavy particles associated with the models, with predicted masses of approximately 1-2 TeV for gluon bosons and 1.5-3 TeV for scalar bosons. The models also predict the annihilation of dark matter particles into various theoretical particles such as bosons and leptons,

We introduce a new technique to identify the emission of molecular lines in vast numbers of galaxies observed through spectroscopic studies at the frequency of 220 GHz, which is particularly effective at detecting specific lines such as CO, HCN(1-0), or CN(1-0) in galaxies with redshifts above 2. This technique will be indispensable for analyzing data from future studies, as it accurately predicts the sensitivity thresholds required to make reliable detections in various redshift ranges. It also takes into account factors such as diverse molecular lines and the time needed for data collection in extensive surveys, all within a framework that adapts to the capacity of upcoming studies, whether small, medium-sized, or massive. This technique is particularly essential for large-scale surveys being conducted at the frequency of 220 GHz in the millimeter-wave range, and it will be equally applicable for analyzing data from other studies, regardless of their frequency, redshift ranges, or sample sizes. The technique is highly versatile and can be used for a wide variety of studies, and it has been applied here to identify robust (sub)mm redshifts in various scenarios, from small to medium and large samples, and from specific to comprehensive redshift ranges.

Our investigation focuses on the dynamical properties of the $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg model on the triangular lattice with $S=1/2$ spins. Using the two-dimensional lattice and incorporating a $J_2$ bond-dependent interaction, the evolution of the dynamical structure factor as a function of $J_2$ is examined. Starting with the primary $J_2=0$ state characterized by a magnetically ordered state within the system, the introduction of a $J_2/J_1$ ratio up to 0.15 leads to a change in the ordered state from a $\sqrt{7\times7$ pattern to a larger $2\times2$ pattern. The evolution of the ordered state is also associated with a shift in the continuum spin excitations at an intermediate $J_2$ ratio of 0.65, resulting in a spin liquid-like behavior. The known spin liquid model based on the Schwinger spin operators, the $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg model, and the structure of the energy excitations all reveal a broken $C_3$ symmetry. The relative magnitudes of the energy excitations based on the $q=0$ and $\pi$ wave vectors are key indicators of the existence of a spin liquid-like behavior within the system.

Utilizing high-performance lattice techniques and cutting-edge algorithms, our research focuses on the $SU(2)$ subset of $SU(3)$ in a diverse array of group representations. Our results reveal the intricate dynamics of the process where a confined state transitions to a deconfined one, specifically at the critical point where the symmetry still retains its gauge structure. This process exhibits distinct characteristics distinguished by the interactions involving triple bosons, thereby shedding new light on the underlying principles of $SU(3)$ gauge theory. To explore this phenomenon in-depth, our research utilizes four distinct representations: the fundamental $2$, the adjoint $3$, and two further representations, $5$ and $15$, which serve as a $SU(2)$ doublet and a $SU(2)$ triplet, respectively, to explore the underlying principles of $SU(3)$ gauge theory. Our findings specifically relate to the critical point $T_c$ where the breaking of $SU(3)$ symmetry still retains its $SU(2)$ content. Our research reveals the process of confinement vs deconfinement to be highly analogous across the diverse array of representations examined. Our results specifically show the process of quark confinement to be directly linked to the energy released upon the boson-triple-coupling process across the critical point $T_c$. This connection is observed to be universally valid across the diverse array of representations examined. This discovery holds significant implications for our comprehension of matter constitution within high-energy and post-c

Cr$_2$Al exhibits a tetragonal Laves phase structure and demonstrates an in-plane magnetic arrangement at high temperatures. The in-plane and out-of-plane exchange interactions were determined through the analysis of neutron diffraction and are comparable in magnitude. The parameters for the in-plane and out-of-plane interactions are $A_{\perp}$ = 0.044 meV and $A_{||}$ = 0.20 meV, respectively, indicating a significantly stronger anisotropy in the former. The magnetic structure of Cr$_2$Al can be effectively described using a Heisenberg model that takes into account spin-wave excitations. The spin-wave spectrum peaks at approximately 15 meV, corresponding to a mean nearest-neighbor distance magnitude of 3.08 Å. The spin wave density of states reveals a distinct peak at high energy, characterized by a energy value of 15 meV, which indicates a significant density of magnetic states.

A microscopic model for two-dimensional rarefied gas flows is developed, where the collision frequency of molecules depends on the relative velocities between molecules. This model uses a simplified expression for the collision term in the Boltzmann equation, based on an extended Fenske-Harrison model. This Fenske-Harrison model calculates the probability of collision for molecules with specific velocities, by summing over virtual virtual velocities of a collision partner. By using this probability in the Boltzmann equation, the model has been successfully compared against Monte Carlo simulations for pressure distributions on a flat plate under various gas flow conditions. This model has also been used to examine the impact of an attractive potential between molecules at low temperatures. Finally, the model's results have been used to examine the impact of attractive potential on velocity distributions, by adjusting the Knudsen number to compare models with and without velocity-dependent collision frequency.

To put it simply, machines struggle to comprehend human-like understanding. A significant challenge in advancing artificial intelligence is creating systems that can learn from examples and experience. The commonly used methods for machine learning in this area often produce systems that can only answer questions based on the data they've been given, rather than applying their knowledge more broadly. 

We present a new approach, called the Naturalized Semantic Interpreter, which aims to simulate human-like learning from scarce information. We demonstrate this approach using two complex tasks: answering questions based on visual images and understanding the implications of written text. We test our method using a limited dataset and show that it successfully generalizes the knowledge it's learned to previously unseen situations. 

A key aspect of our approach involves representing meanings in a way that captures their relationships and commonalies, which enables the model to update its understanding of concepts that have multiple associated features. We compare our method to more traditional forms of machine learning and show that it produces more accurate results on tasks such as recognizing objects in images and Implication Learning. The results indicate that our method achieves a higher level of understanding than typical machine learning techniques, which prioritize training models on specific, isolated tasks.

The Electron-Ion Collider's future will involve utilizing electron-proton and electron-nucleus collisions to advance our understanding of quarks and gluons in conjunction with quantum chromodynamics. To achieve precise measurements of key properties, forward-jet veto detectors and forward tagging systems are being integrated for assessment in the initial EIC design. Given the prominence of gluon-driven processes in electron-nucleus collisions, incorporating a forward tagging system becomes essential, as observed in previous deep inelastic scattering experiments. Advances have been made in forward silicon tracking sensors for particle physics experiments, including LHC upgrades and a proposed ILC. Prototypes for forward tracking sensors, incorporating CMOS technology, have been developed and optimized for the EIC's forward tagging system, as described within this article.

A significant drop of nearly 50% in the brightness of the galaxy M60 USS, which houses an extremely low-mass supermassive black hole, led us to investigate whether its observed variability is due to a black hole or another type of active galactic nucleus. By analyzing M60 USS's light output using the Z-SPT camera, we discovered that its power spectrum exhibits a significant level of variability at a frequency of approximately 0.04 day^-1. This same variability frequency matches the one found in the time-based changes of a starburst galactic nucleus, suggesting that the galaxy UGC 10276 might be an alternative explanation for M60 USS's light fluctuations. Combining the data from multiple frequency bands, we were able to identify several key components, including a black hole with a mass of about 10^6 solar masses as well as a massive star-forming system, which accounts for around one-fifth of the observed infrared radiation of the galaxy. By assuming an energetic balance between the galaxy's infrared radiation and the energy released from the massive star-forming system, which causes the light from the starburst to absorb or scatter at a nearby area, we were able to calculate that the massive star-forming system in the galaxy M60 USS erupts around a few thousand years. The overall pattern of a star's magnetic field is still largely unclear. Studies have primarily focused on the surface features of magnetic field patterns, whereas its deeper structures remain largely unknown. In this research, we have made an effort to map the magnetic field's slope within a specific layer of the star HD58260 through in-depth spectral analysis. Our analysis relied on the spectral properties of certain lines that react differently to various field depths. It was discovered that the magnetic field's intensity decreases as it moves towards the star's surface, with a gradient of -0.8 gauss per radial distance. This star's magnetic field intensity is relatively weak, with a surface field intensity of approximately 50 Gauss. In contrast, the magnetic field loops' peak intensity reaches up to 1000 Gauss. It was observed that the magnetic field's temperature sensitivity significantly influences its spectral features. In cases where the magnetic field's intensity is high, its thermal properties tend to suppress its thermal equilibrium, resulting in less accurate models of its thermal state. In order to accurately map the magnetic field's slope, it is necessary to employ a model that accurately reflects the magnetic field's thermal and velocity state, with a model error of less than 2% over a 2000 Kelvin temperature range. Our findings also highlight the importance of adjusting the model's line width error in accordance with its thermal and velocity state in order to accurately map the magnetic field's slope. A representation of the Dunkl operator over the real numbers, involving free bosons, has specific characteristics when the parameter is set to one. For arbitrary parameters, there is a connection to the Calogero model, specifically its one-dimensional case with specific potential values related to the parameter's power of the coordinate. Furthermore, for parameter values greater than one, a specific decoupling of the system's modes occurs in the space of its eigenfunctions.

Using ALMA's high sensitivity and compact array, we've made detailed measurements of the H30α line emission in NGC 5233, a nearby dwarf galaxy with very low metal content. These observations enable us to assess the role of the C18O(3-2) emission, previously used as a star formation indicator, as a tracer. We've successfully identified 15 distinct H30α emission regions within the central 350pc, including 6 that have been previously mapped at higher frequencies. Our analysis compares the C18O(3-2) and H30α fluxes against each other and against other star formation indicators. We find significant differences in the distributions of C18O(3-2) and H30α outside a radius of 150pc. This suggests that the C18O(3-2) emission was largely absent due to the warmer temperatures. We observe a stronger correlation in the H30α flux in the central region when compared to the Hα flux, indicating that they share a common power source through a density dependent conversion process. We found a relatively lower ratio when comparing H30α to 12CO(1-0), in comparison to the central region when compared to the H30α flux, indicating that the CO is not a reliable indicator of the star formation in the region.
