The Nirenberg problem on a half sphere minimizes a functional that combines a scalar curvature term with a total mean curvature term, subject to constraints on the trace-free mean curvature and a Neumann boundary condition. We demonstrate that non-trivial minimal solutions exist for this problem when 3 or 4 dimensions are considered.

Deep Learning models' success relies heavily on effective representation learning, but the conventional measures of representation quality are limited in their capabilities. They fail to account for various complex factors that can affect performance, leading to suboptimal results in some cases. This study introduces a new performance metric for deep models, one that accounts for the relationships between different classes and uses the Kullback-Leibler Divergence alongside the Wasserstein distance and the sinkhorn divergence. It also proposes a novel training objective for deep models, taking into consideration the inter-class correlations and uses a combination of the KL-divergence, W-divergence, and s-divergence. The proposed metric and objective have been tested on various datasets, demonstrating improved performance and reduced dependence on data standardisation. The results indicate that models trained with the proposed objective and metric show better representation quality and are more generalisable. They also demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on various benchmark datasets.

In England, a comprehensive contact tracing system was established to curb the spread of COVID-19 by identifying and isolating infected individuals' close contacts. The trace was executed by the National Health Service Test and Trace service and supported by local partners. This research aimed to examine how involvement of these local partners influenced the test and trace service's effectiveness. Using data on COVID-19 infections between September 1, 2020, and January 31, 2021, in 149 local areas in England, the analysis compared test and trace performance under the national and local partnership models. The results indicated that local partnerships enhanced the test and trace service's efficiency, particularly in areas with lower socioeconomic status and higher prevalence of COVID-19 infections, by improving the national Test and Trace service's coverage of infected individuals' close contacts by up to 30-40%. The study also found that local partnerships complemented the national Test and Trace service, addressing challenges and enhancing its overall effectiveness during the pandemic's critical phase. The analysis provided the first empirical assessment of the local partnership model's impact on the test and trace service's performance.

Determining the fundamental parameters of star clusters is a vital component of astrophysical research. Utilizing the Gaia DR2 survey provides an opportunity for precise assessments of star positions, parallax, and motion based on uniform photometric data, thus enabling the determination of accurate cluster membership probabilities. Focused on the Melotte 72 open star cluster, this study employs Gaia DR2 data to derive fundamental cluster data points, including radial velocity, distance, age, and mass, supplemented by additional information sources, including the Telescopio Vaporesso survey. Results indicate a uniform distance for Melotte 72 of around 2395+/-45 parsecs based on multiple methods as well as a similar range of metallic content. With radial velocities measured from several studies, a consistent range of metal content and radial velocities for Melotte 72 are observed. Moreover, a consistent age and mass estimates for the Melotte 72 open star cluster of around 700 million years and 5000-6000 solar masses respectively, are derived through various methods.

We examine random point sets $X_n$ resulting from independent and identically distributed random variables in $\mathbb{R}^q$ with a H\"older continuous density. When the dimension $q$ grows exponentially with $n$ and the degree of H\"older continuity $\alpha$ is at least 1, we establish an approximation for the expected value of the $i^{th}$ Betti number of the Delaunay complex, which we denote as $\mathbb{E} \beta_i(X_n)$. This expected value is calculated as a product of two factors, where the first is the binomial coefficient binomial$(n-1, i)$ and the second depends on the point density $\rho_n$ of $X_n$. The point density $\rho_n$ represents a convolution of the original point density $\rho$ with itself $i+1$ times. When the point density $\rho$ has a finite second moment and the distance between successive points in $X_n$ has a finite first moment, we utilize a Poisson process approximation and demonstrate the convergence in law of the Delaunay complex with respect to a certain metric. As a result, we obtain the desired approximation for $\mathbb{E} \beta_i(X_n)$. When the point density $\rho$ has a finite third moment, we employ a Berstein-von Mises type argument to establish the convergence in law of the empirical point density towards its corresponding Gaussian distribution

We address the issue of adjusting an eye-in-hand camera in tasks like 3D manipulation by leveraging a single image. Our method makes three key contributions: 1) we develop a practical simulation environment that accounts for camera movements and image reflections; 2) we design a network that integrates geometric constraints and appearance information to estimate camera poses; 3) we propose a refinement mechanism to enhance accuracy and resilience to image distortions. Experimental results demonstrate that our method effectively calculates accurate camera poses, even in cases with significant image perturbations. Moreover, our approach enables 3D manipulation capabilities, including object picking. Our findings provide valuable insights for implementing effective 3D manipulation systems in complex real-world scenarios.

In reversal learning, we examine tasks where a learner must mimic a skilled user's behaviors to obtain rewards, with the key difference being that the learner can observe the consequences of the expert's actions but cannot directly view the actions themselves. This concept of reversal learning poses significant computational challenges that necessitate novel solution approaches. Given the distinct nature of this problem in comparison to traditional reinforcement learning tasks, we have dubbed it Reverse Learning or RL. Our investigation into RL reveals that aligning with the expert's outcomes is insufficient to guarantee optimal actions. Consequently, we propose a novel framework that integrates constraint theory to keep RL actions in sync with the expert's hypothetical policy. Our theoretical analysis confirms the efficacy of this approach, and through simulations within two diverse environments, we have found that RL performs at par with direct learning in our framework, while also outperforming a control condition that solely seeks to mirror the expert's outcomes.

The European Space Agency's GAIA mission has released its Data Release 2 (DR2), a groundbreaking dataset that provides precise celestial coordinates and movement information for approximately one percent of the galaxy's stars. This report offers an overview of the mission, highlighting its scientific and technical achievements in preparing DR2 for analysis. This can be accomplished through the application of novel and efficient methods of data processing, some of which are presented here in detail. These efforts have allowed the mission to achieve remarkable accuracy in measuring stars' parallax, which offers a unique opportunity for conducting groundbreaking research across various scientific fields including the study of the galaxy's structure.

For tree-decomposition-based algorithms, vertex division is a crucial technique but it can occupy a substantial amount of space. To address this issue, researchers have proposed an improved, space-efficient vertex divider based on balanced separators, which has a specific space requirement determined by the treewidth and the number of separators. To optimize the divider's performance, they have developed an alternative, two-phase approach that first determines a balanced separator using O(|H|) space and then identifies the divider using that separator while only storing the critical treewidth parameter and separator details, totaling O(|H| + tw) space, where tw is the treewidth. To demonstrate its applicability, they have created a unified algorithm for solving graph problems, such as testing graph isomorphism, which has the same optimal space efficiency as the best known methods except when the treewidth requires |H| + tw = O(n log^2 n) bits, which occurs in rare cases where the treewidth is substantially affected by the height of the treewidth-based tree-decomposition.

Network analysis through visualization offers significant insights but comes with its limitations, particularly when dealing with large datasets that can overwhelm due to the abundance of information they contain. To rectify this issue, various methods have been developed to represent complex networks in a more manageable form, such as those with extensive amounts of data. This paper delves into existing interpretations and requirements for weighted network visualization, with a specific focus on organizing elements into manageable groups. It has become necessary to cater to networks that aren't merely composed of nodes with varying connections, but also those with inherent errors or lacking complete information regarding node relationships. To address these shortcomings, we've established new criteria for directed network visualization, with a particular focus on incorporating node heterogeneity, accommodating missing information, and ensuring the integrity of visualizations. We've also demonstrated the effectiveness of our proposed methods through practical applications and highlighted their applications in real-world scenarios.

One notable advantage of using neural networks to solve partial differential equations (PDEs) is their ability to approximate complex functions with ease, similar to traditional Volterra and Hammerstein networks, used extensively in the past. With the inclusion of physics-aware data, such as initial and boundary conditions, PDE-based neural networks can offer superior performance and precision, particularly when combined with high-accuracy numerical methods for certain parts of the problem. 

Our study focuses on the development of an error estimation technique for physics-aware neural networks. By utilizing a combination of the neural network and a physics-based initial and boundary condition solver, such as the finite element method, we can achieve highly accurate PDE solutions with the assurance of a quantifiable level of error. This approach has been demonstrated on a range of PDE problems including those influenced by biharmonic and Poisson interactions.

Epidemiologic studies heavily rely on air quality indicators to establish the links between atmospheric pollution and the occurrence of diseases. In recent years, big data analytics and machine learning have emerged as key elements in creating population exposure maps. This exposure data serves as the groundwork for making inferences regarding the population, including those residing in urban and rural areas. In this context, we investigate two methods for predicting air pollution indicators. The first approach relies on combining two types of spatial data analysis models: the EM algorithm, which uses AMO model's regression framework to estimate the mean background concentration, and the k-NN model, which provides local adjustments to the model's predictions. The second method involves training a multi-layer neural network, specifically a graph neural network type, to predict the concentration of pollutants from a selection of population features. We evaluate the performance of these methods by analyzing predictive models for NOx concentration created using different sets of population features.

A Majorana spectrum typically stands out among other spectra due to its distinct N+1 rule where the amplitude of certain magnetically modulated conductance peaks relates to the strength of magnetic field flux within the system's core. However, previous theoretical studies indicated that introducing ohmic dissipation into the system would compromise the uniqueness of the observed peaks, rendering identification based solely on the peak's amplitude shape ineffective. Consequently, the problem of distinguishing a Majorana's conductance signature from other non-Majorana signatures became unresolved. This study proposes a comprehensive solution to overcome this challenge by employing a combination of two processes: the first involves detecting the shift in the conductance peak's position under a specific magnetic field, and the second entails identifying the magnetically-induced conductance minimum that occurs near the core of topological superconducting island systems, ultimately allowing for the unambiguous identification of a Majorana's conductance signature in the presence of ohmic dissipation.

We analyzed the linear bandits issue, characterized by a set of actions in a high-dimensional space, each with its own feature vector. The unknown size and properties of this set were considered. We established an optimal upper bound for the rate of pseudo-dimension growth in linear bandits, providing a dynamic criterion for action sets. This criterion states that if pseudo-dimension is less than $\epsilon N$ and action radius is less than $R$, then expected regret will be upper bounded by $K R^2 \ln(N) / \epsilon$ after $N$ time steps. This bound is close to optimal, as it falls short by at most $K R^2$. We further tested a specific instance where actions form a grid in $d$-dimensional space with $M$ elements per dimension. We determined the minimum sample size needed to achieve sub-logarithmic regret by taking the maximum of $M^2 d$ and $\ln^2 N$. The results were compared with previously proposed methods, yielding regret bounds that fall short by at most $M^2$. We then employed a statistical inference technique, similar to Blei et al. (2017), to derive regret bounds for linear bandits. The proposed inference-based approach enjoys an improvement in regret, compared to the pseudo-dimension based upper bounds.

Graphene with gaps, as in silicene, exhibits the valley Hall effect, a consequence of broken spatial inversions symmetries. We propose an alternative explanation for a notable current flowing through the gaps, attributing it to a unique oral topological property unique to gapped graphene. By treating rotations as a fundamental symmetry, we demonstrate that a specific type of transition, known as the Berry phase, is implemented in gapped graphene. As a result, an oral topological charge generates a significant flow, analogous to the valley Hall effect previously observed in gapped materials. We predict that within an external magnetic field, the oral Hall effect surpasses the valley Hall effect in gapped materials in terms of magnitude.

Machine learning models' effectiveness in real-world settings can be severely impacted by data contamination, which occurs when training data includes inaccurate or misleading information. The financial sector, for instance, may have problems with label noise caused by disagreeing judges. Unlike masking techniques, which can be used to counteract label variation, data contamination simulates the unavailability of clean data, making it difficult to determine the most accurate model. We propose a framework that uses reinforcement learning to maximize the performance of models dealing with data contamination, and this framework automatically allocates a score to each model being trained. The score represents the expected model's performance if it were trained on clean data. The framework involves graph neural networks models, black-box evaluators, and a reinforcement learning strategy to find the optimal level of data contamination, and a baseline model to compare results. We tested our framework on datasets with different types of contamination and found that it consistently outperformed traditional methods.

The process of matching object catalogs relies on cross-identification to link objects between different catalogs. This procedure often needs to be repeated and updated, especially when new catalogs become available or are added. To cross-identify objects, a statistical approach, such as the \Si algorithm, is commonly employed, which utilizes astrometry to calculate a match probability score. Building upon this concept, we introduce two new techniques that combine astrometry with photometric data to cross-identify objects. These methods, which are based on the probability of two objects being the same, are either used to correct the position of one catalog based on the other, or by each catalog eliminating unlikely matches to the best-fit objects. We test and validate these techniques using simulated and real data, particularly the two versions of the \HSA catalog, astrometric and photometric, against the \Gaia Early third data release. The outcomes demonstrate that incorporating photometric information not only reduces the number of false matches compared to using only astrometry but also identifies a more plausible match in some instances where the score indicates a low match probability.

In a hypergraph, the size of the smallest vertex subset that encompasses at least
$e$ distinct edges is known as the $e$-minimal size of the subset. For every $e$, there
exists an $e$-monohapax hypergraph, meaning it has just one dominant edge, with its
minimal size equal to $e$. However, for certain values of $e$, there may exist
$e$-monohapax hypergraphs where the minimal size of the dominating edge within
monohapax extensions is less than $e$. We explore the limits of $e$-monohapax and
$e$-bipartite hypergraphs and their properties in this study.

Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, formally structured concept relationships called ontologies. In fields like biology and medicine, vast ontologies consist of millions of interconnected concepts. Effective visualization tools are greatly needed for navigating and understanding the intricate structure of such large ontologies. Currently, available visualization methods mainly focus on hierarchical relationships, leaving the analysis of non-hierarchical connections and their interactions with hierarchical structures largely neglected. To address this gap, we present OntoPlot, a novel visual representation that clearly differentiates and displays both hierarchical and non-hierarchical connections within ontologies. A prototype system has been developed and thoroughly tested, showcasing its capabilities with real-world examples from the Biological Ontology.

We introduce an innovative technique that combines extreme multi-label classification and inter-domain losses with CycleGAN to exploit latent information in unsupervised domain adaptation for end-to-end automatic speech recognition. This approach can handle diverse tasks and resources without requiring additional training data, significantly reducing the need for manual annotation. We test its effectiveness using two sets of unlabeled data, specifically Korean data processed by TTS models and a large Chinese speech corpus, showing substantial improvements in speech recognition performance, with a significant gain of 4.73% in clean conditions.

This study introduces a novel method of navigation for autonomous robots that leverages deep active prediction. The approach relies on a predictive model of the robot's target, which dynamically adjusts its policy to optimize performance based on current estimates of target dynamics. By incorporating an influenced policy, the framework minimizes the need for complex reinforcement learning. The effectiveness of this deep active prediction method is demonstrated through successful navigation of a mobile robot in diverse simulated environments.

Our research focuses on the Soret effect, a phenomenon where a concentration gradient in a system leads to fluid flow. We examine this effect not just in bulk fluids, but also in nanoscale systems. To do this, we utilize molecular dynamics simulations of flexible molecules in 2D and 3D systems, and discover that the Soret effect has a significant contribution from the flexible internal degrees of freedom. The strength of this contribution varies depending on the molecules' flexibility and spatial scope. Interestingly, we find that introducing noise into our simulations can aid in achieving stable, thermodynamically harmonic diffusion even at a nanoscale, and significantly enhance the Soret effect's magnitude.

The capability to automatically evaluate large quantities of written work has long been a significant challenge due to its inherent complexity and time-consuming nature for human assessment. Recent advancements in natural language processing using transformer models have provided enhanced capabilities for text comprehension and analysis. This study utilizes a dataset collected from actual exams to compare the efficacy of various language models for automated written work assessment. It is demonstrated that combining multiple models leads to superior overall performance and more reliable results when compared to relying on a single powerful model. Additionally, the study examines the advantages of leveraging written responses over descriptive questions for automated assessment.

One of the significant drawbacks of deep pedestrian detection methods is that they yield a large number of false positives, especially when adapted to a new environment. This challenge becomes even more pronounced when working with unlabeled domain shift scenarios, where there's no viable approach to tackle the resulting performance drop. In response to this issue, we propose a novel technique that employs an unsupervised framework to reduce false positives at various stages of the detection pipeline. First, we develop an unsupervised positive pruning method that eliminates easy positives through self-supervision, thereby enhancing the quality of positive proposals. Next, we introduce a novel ranking criterion for box prediction, which is trained without any supervision and prioritizes the remaining positive proposals based on their box predictions. Finally, we establish a new metric space that minimizes the distance between positive and negative boxes, thereby reducing false positives. This novel framework, called the Box Re-Ranking Network (BRRN), is highly efficient and effective in domain adaptive pedestrian detection. When applied to a standard pipeline, it yields substantial performance improvements, with an average increase of 3.7% AP bound. When used in conjunction with commonly employed domain adaptation methods, BRRN further boosts performance by 6.8% AP on average. Comprehensive ablation studies demonstrate that each component of the Box Re-Ranking Network yields significant improvements in domain adaptive pedestrian detection. The code and model for this research are publicly available at https://github.com/whi1033/Box-Re-Ranking

This study presents an innovative method for enhancing low-quality music recordings made on mobile devices, which often suffer from distortion such as background noise, echo effects, and poor microphone placement. To counter these issues, a novel deep learning approach combines two techniques: an image-to-image translation model that removes noise and transforms into a suitable waveform, and a vocoder that converts the modified waveform into a high-quality audio format. To evaluate the effectiveness of this method, a custom dataset was created using a widely available noise-reducing model and 15 distinct types of real-world background noises, which were added to music recordings. By comparing the results, it is clear that our approach significantly outperforms existing noise-reduction models.

Our research focuses on the impact of a virtual ball's Point of Release on the percepion of a throwing motion. We define this Point of Release as the instant when the ball leaves the thrower's hand. An inaccurate representation of the Point of Release distorts the thrower's character model, thereby altering the motion. An attempt to simulate a throwing motion from any point other than the correct Point of Release results in a ball trajectory that deviates from the intended. Ultimately, the ball might land in an unrealistic location. In this study, viewers' capacity to identify an incorrect throwing motion is investigated. Five expert animators and 35 average viewers watched throwing motion videos where the Point of Release was either accurately or inaccurately represented. The resulting observations led to the development of FauxThrow, a web-based platform where users can share their assessments of the majority of the tested throwing motions. The collective feedback revealed that only one out of the 35 average viewers could pinpoint an inaccurately represented Point of Release in a throwing motion. In contrast, all five expert animators successfully identified the inaccuracies. The results suggest that the presence of a throwing motion with a clearly inaccurate Point of Release may serve as a distinct indicator of a poorly executed motion, implying that even average individuals can reliably detect such errors.

A novel decoding approach utilizing a tree structured vocabulary and a redefined similarity metric for alignment has been proposed. By building upon a parental graph with predetermined rules, a limited number of possible child relationships for each word are identified. This tree structured vocabulary decoder is then used in conjunction with a reinterpreted similarity metric to determine the most suitable tree based on starting word, parental status, and sequence context. A 'best child' criterion is employed for handling words without child relationships, thereby ensuring decoding efficiency. Notably, this top-down tree structured decoding approach outperforms existing methods in both translation and parsing tasks.

The formation of molecular complexes in interstellar clouds and disks influences various aspects of astrochemistry, including the creation of chemically reactive species and the emission of light in the electromagnetic spectrum. Theoretical models of these complexes often rely on the energy released when atoms bond, which can vary based on different mathematical approaches and computational settings. The new Binding Energy Assessment Platform provides a database of molecular bond energy values, allowing users to explore both the methods used to obtain these values and the impact of these methods on astrochemical results, including model predictions and the formation of complex molecules in dense interstellar clouds. By promoting discussion and clarification of the use and impact of molecular bond energy values, this platform supports more accurate and comprehensive astrochemical modeling.

A multiplicative stochastic process is studied, where a randomly assigned geometric factor, based on a uniform probability distribution between 0.1 and 1, is applied to the original sample value, resulting in the new value. This concept's practical applications are explored, with specific emphasis on its potential use in the generation of random numbers. Specifically, this process can be utilized within algorithms employing the Monte Carlo technique, such as the Monte Carlo simulation for option pricing, for instance in the model developed by Binomial, where the stochastic factor would affect the asset price progression step.

We propose a time-efficient approach to calculate the expected value of any polynomial function by applying random Clifford circuits with a low number of layers. Building upon this, we develop an algorithm that achieves a significant speed-up in evaluating higher-order polynomial functions, leveraging the benefits of this structure. However, this technique yields a linear time complexity for evaluating cubic functions, which is comparable to the optimal quadratic time complexity but falls short of the linear threshold time complexity achievable through direct calculation. Notably, we are also unable to adapt this technique to support the assessment of individual instances within a fixed polynomial function.

For the Davey-Stewartson II equation with two-dimensional water waves, the reflection coefficient has been calculated and further studied its behavior as the wavenumber's absolute value increases. In doing so, a Birkhoff norm has been defined and used in conjunction with the equation's evolution invariant norms to establish growth estimates for solutions with large wavennumbers. In turn, these estimates led to the reflection coefficient's behavior as the wavennumber's absolute value grows being examined, where it was discovered that it behaves differently based on whether the wavennumber's imaginary part is greater than or equal to the real part. In cases where the real part is greater than the imaginary part, the reflection coefficient exhibits a behavior that is characteristic of one-dimensional Schrodinger equations. Conversely, when the real part is less than the imaginary part, the reflection coefficient behaves differently and may or may not tend towards zero as the wavennumber's absolute value increases. In order to investigate this behavior, a non-convex duality theorem was employed in conjunction with the equation's coefficients.

Recent text classification models' output distributions often become disrupted due to input anomalies such as poisoned data, causing serious issues for models deployed in high-stakes domains like healthcare. We develop novel variants of the Sibyl anomaly detection framework to address this problem by quantifying the anomaly level of each training example and identifying and removed anomalous data points. Experiments on multiple datasets show that our proposed approach, which removes anomalous data points, significantly improves text classification robustness and output reliability.

In the realm of shallow learning, linear models are a fundamental tool, yet they often prove ineffective for deep neural networks. However, traditional representation learning methods struggle to adapt and are generally ineffective in a variety of settings. Our breakthrough lies in an innovative form of representation learning that acknowledges the intricacies of deep neural networks. By utilizing the principles of kernel methods and low-rank approximations, this approach yields a linear representation suitable for a range of deep learning models. Notably, our technique lends itself perfectly to meta-learning, allowing for training on small datasets and effortlessly adapting to never-seen tasks from limited, unlabeled data. Through comprehensive testing on multiple domains, our method consistently ranks among the best representation choices. Furthermore, we showcase its effectiveness in zero-shot learning settings, as well as its ability to simplify feature extraction from complex networks.

Building lightweight multilingual machine translation models for low-resource languages and leveraging model compression through quantization and distillation has become a pressing issue. While they offer promising approaches to tackle this problem, the success of model compression is highly dependent on the characteristics of the models in question. Unfortunately, there is a lack of in-depth research exploring the impact of model compression on neural machine translation for low-resource languages, especially under limited data conditions. This work aims to fill this gap by investigating how effective quantization and distillation are in compressing low-resource MT models and optimizing them for their respective languages. Additionally, we examine the impact of model compression on the performance of state-of-the-art MT models in cross-lingual representation learning. We conduct an extensive exploration of model compression techniques, evaluating a total of 78 combinations of model compression methods, learning rates, and optimization algorithms on four different languages, ultimately discovering that an optimized distillation approach results in significant improvements in translation quality. Importantly, we highlight the inherent fragility of using distillation for model compression, emphasizing the need for thorough research into the optimal model compression strategy when developing and optimizing low-resource MT models and models of cross-lingual representation.

A hypergraph is a collection of hyperedges connecting vertices in a higher dimensional space than a standard graph. We can think of the vertices as locations and hyperedges as broader areas within a 2-dimensional plane. The density of a hypergraph is calculated by dividing the total area of its hyperedges by the area occupied by its vertices. However, this measurement can be misleading due to the potential for smaller hyperedges to dominate the outcome, even if they are overshadowed by larger ones. The focus of this paper is on the logical and illogical densities of hypergraphs, which is determined by the ratio of their planar areas over their planar areas excluding the hyperedges, respectively. We begin by proving that every hypergraph has a single illogical Lagrangian density. Next, we demonstrate that the overall illogical density of a hypergraph paired with n identical copies of itself is equal to n and confirm that the same relationship holds for paired logical densities. These findings are significant because they illustrate that the illogical density is a stable characteristic that endures through various duplications, in contrast to the logical density, which we also show can be any real number between 0 and 1 inclusive. The paper's conclusions are visually illustrated through a pair of hypergraphs with illogical densities of 1/2 and 2, showcasing the phenomenon of density inversion through duplication.

Various applications using computer vision have underlined the necessity for effective image segmentation techniques. Deep learning algorithms, particularly fully convolutional networks (FCNs), have been widely utilized in image segmentation tasks, achieving impressive results. However, employing DL algorithms in clinical settings is often hindered by the labor-intensive process of collecting and labeling medical data. To address this issue, we investigated the utilization of data augmentation techniques, specifically for pneumonia detection, to minimize the required amount of labeled data needed for training an FCN model.

Capable image description systems produce diverse and accurate descriptions 
for various scenes, yet the current state of the art often falls short in 
providing descriptions that are tailored to specific contexts or tastes. This 
shortcoming hampers the utility of image description systems in real-world 
applications. To address this limitation, we propose CIDD, a prompting-based 
framework that enables fine-grained control over image description generation. 
Unlike existing systems, CIDD facilitates description generation within 
various linguistic styles and levels of detail. Unlike conventional image 
description models that necessitate comprehensive retraining for even minor 
modifications, CIDD employs a controllable and efficient prompting mechanism 
that facilitates flexible modification. Experimental results demonstrate that 
our method produces descriptions consistent with human standards and surpass 
state-of-the-art benchmarks. This study is publicly available at 
https://github.com/Algebraic-mind/CIDD.

This paper delves into the concept of harm, often a secondary consideration behind utility maximization, but lately, some authors have argued that harm should be a primary moral concern. Our investigation aims to clarify the nature of harm as a moral consideration and to distinguish its various aspects. One aspect we identify is adverse consequences, but we argue that harm caused by consequences is not unique to moral consideration and can be evaluated through a causal analysis. On the other hand, some cases of harm stem from what we term a agent's mindset, and we claim this type of consideration is peculiar to moral evaluation.

This study showcases the integration of MMLSpark, a spark-based open source library, in a deep learning project. In the context of traffic sign classification, we implement adaptable and scalable techniques that combine the strengths of TensorFlow and Microsoft's Machine Learning libraries with Python coding. Specifically, we utilize MMLSpark's spark-ml and tensorflow-mr modules to leverage their ml-main and tfmr image processing capabilities.

We introduce a pioneering task known as zero-shot voice translation, where an audio signal from one language is translated into the spoken form of another language. To tackle this challenge, we develop a robust model architecture incorporating advanced features like attention, which can be trained on a large corpus of audio-data paired with multiple languages. By designing a zero-shot voice translation framework based on transformer networks, we are able to translate signals from one language into others without needing to prepare a separate dataset for each possible source language. To overcome the difficulty in processing audio data, we employ a continuous speech embedding system based on self-attention. To our knowledge, this ambitious task has not been attempted previously and we provide a starting point for further research in this unexplored area.

This work aims to expand upon previous research by modifying the standard heat equation to include phase transitions across temperature changes. In contrast to other studies, the phase transition boundary conditions will shift over time. Building on the work of Coleman and Gurtin, the new model will take into account both thermal memory and moving boundary changes. Two key aspects will be explored: first, the model boundaries will change in accordance with temperature changes while maintaining independence from thermal memory, and second, the model will remain stress-free. Two methods will be employed to demonstrate that the model will result in a heat flux defined by a heat function, a stress function, and a function representing the rate of boundary change. These functions will be further linked to temperature-dependent functions, and the model will be solved using a numerical method when both sides of the model boundary are subject to the same temperature changes. In addition, the model will be tested for validity by comparing its results with those from a model featuring non-moving boundaries. In order to demonstrate the model's practical application, the model will be used to simulate a solid plate cooling process.

We aim to enhance the accuracy of short-term load forecasting, particularly for low voltage networks, by combining the strengths of model-based and curve-fitting forecasting techniques. Our study combines an ARMAX-EST model, which uses historical data and integral coefficients to forecast normal load levels, with the ILSF-ARMAX-EST model, which incorporates additional information to forecast peak hours and reduces low-load forecasting errors. By integrating these models into a probabilistic framework, we obtain a fused forecast and quantify the forecast uncertainty using a Gaussian distribution. Our approach yields significant improvements in forecast accuracy, particularly for high-load periods.

Deep learning successes have sparked widespread use of machine learning algorithms in engineering and science. Despite the considerable outcomes, many scientists remain skeptical regarding the reliability and interpretability of these models. In the scientific community, model interpretability and transparency are essential features for validating model results. In this report, advanced machine learning and deep learning methods are introduced, along with protocols for assessing model performance and reliability. A step-by-step guide is provided for integrating domain-specific knowledge into machine learning model development. Furthermore, model interpretability and transparency are discussed, and a comparison of different approaches to validate model results is presented.

The availability of COVID-19 distribution data relies heavily on chest CT scans.
Accurate detection, segmentation, and quantification of pulmonary lesions in 
chest images is critical for disease diagnosis, treatment, and monitoring.
Localizing and identifying pulmonary lesions in fully supervised learning formats 
involves time-consuming annotation processes.
This issue has limited the application of deep learning algorithms in chest images.
Recent research in weakly supervised learning offers an effective solution to 
reduce annotation requirements and improve efficiency.
This paper assesses the performance of different WSL techniques for WCL analysis 
in chest images, with specific focus on WCL-COVID, a new dataset combining 
COVID-19 distribution data with limited boundary annotations.
Using deep learning algorithms, the results reveal that area-based metrics outperform 
classification performance.
Comparative evaluation of different WSL methods reveals that multi-instance 
learning yields better results in terms of precision, recall, and the F1 score.
Finally, the study evaluates the performance of different WSL methods in terms of 
localization and segmentation performance.

A new, automated method for detecting and organizing vertebrae in spinal CT images is introduced. The system uses an optimized, model-based approach to rectify the spine and promote connectedness, effectively localizing the vertebrae. The proposed algorithm is highly reliable, requiring minimal user input, and outperforms previous systems in identifying the vertebrae. Evaluation with a large dataset demonstrates 99% accuracy in identifying individual vertebrae and 98% accuracy in linking them in a sequence.

Electron interactions with a rapidly changing light field in a confined space cause temporary fluctuations in the electron's potential energy. This temporary potential influences can be compared to an adjustable barrier that affects the electron's movement. This, in turn, can alter the electron's probability of crossing a potential barrier that would otherwise be too high to cross. This study examines how these temporary influences affect the electron's behavior when interacting with a light field that resonates with the electron's energy, comparing it to a scenario where the electron's energy is out of sync with the light field's frequency. When the electron's energy is out of sync, its movement is largely unchanged by the temporary potential influences. However, when the electron's energy matches the light field's frequency, its temporary and steady-state movement becomes intertwined with the light field's behavior. Notably, at specific instances when the temporary potential influences peak, an adjustable barrier can be formed that can completely block the electron's path, even from high-energy states. This phenomenon has the potential to be utilized in future nanotechnology by harnessing it to store high-energy electrons in future devices.

Research in quadruped locomotion has gained significant interest in the field of autonomous systems, where the integration of elastic actuators in robotic legs presents an opportunity to reduce weight and decrease the cost of leg systems. There are, however, limitations to using elastic actuators in their current form. They can cause uncomfortable movements in the legs of operating robots due to their elasticity can cause unexpected peak forces that may break delicate sensors and impair the movement planning. To overcome these challenges, this research aims to develop models and movement planners that effectively use elastic actuators in quadruped locomotion. First, an empirical model was created to simulate the interaction between elastic actuators, foot contact, and skeletal structure. This research then developed a movement planner that considers the actuator's elasticity to produce optimal movement. To test the developed models, a simulator of the four-legged robot Spot was utilized to train neural networks to solve a control problem. Experiments have shown that using elastic actuators can enhance the mobility of the robot by implementing various tactics such as utilizing its elasticity to boost the robot's speed during sprints, reducing impact by flexing the legs during landing to decrease wear and tear on delicate components, maintaining consistent posture during quadruped walking in various environments, and navigating through obstacles by flexing the legs during an oblique movement.

A new approach has been developed for resolving the quantum separability problem, 
which involves transforming a non-separable state into a separable state within a 
quantum system characterized by multiple components. The proposed method utilizes 
a specific game to identify the optimal strategy in separating the state's components 
while adhering to given constraints. An improved method has also been introduced, 
which improves the initial approach by incorporating available constraints. It is 
observed that the game's minimax value serves as an effective measure for the state's 
distance from separability, effectively categorizing non-separable states based on 
different criteria. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for a state with certain criteria 
within a one-parameter family, there exists a strategic optimal solution that effectively 
separates its components. An iterative minimization method has also been devised for 
disentangling non-separable states and numerical testing using specific examples has 
confirmed its effectiveness.

This study analyzed the microscopic physical processes underlying a specific instability known as the ripping mode in a collisionless plasma. The code-based investigation revealed that this instability is characterized by modes with very small scales. The mode's amplitude grows rapidly at first, driven by electron temperature fluctuations, before slowing down as it reaches its peak. The code identified three key nonlinear processes influencing the ripping mode. The first one involves a strong magnetic field alignment, driven by current, which limits the mode's growth. The second one is a process where electrons collide to regulate the mode's growth. The code could only account for this collision process. The third one is a process known as electron heating, although this was not a focus of this particular code run.

The fashion industry is vast and lucrative, driven by the development of new and appealing products that rely heavily on image retrieval technologies. Advances in image processing technologies now allow for the manipulation of image features, and as a result, new challenges and opportunities have arisen for search algorithms. This research proposes a novel algorithm that enables fashion brands to create unique, semi-autonomous products by embedding specific features into fashion images. A key aspect of this system is a new, feature-level trait manipulation method that maintains image integrity while allowing for the insertion or modification of distinct features. Evaluation of this approach on the Zalando dataset revealed improved results, and as an added benefit, this system is capable of supporting partial feature manipulation, allowing for more sophisticated applications.

The paper addresses the task of recovering exact data from incomplete and inaccurately measured values, within a known range. It presents a new approach, leveraging dual gradient methods to solve a broad category of ill-posed problems. This broad category involves various types of inverse problems, characterized by different regularity assumptions. The proposed method is tested on combined smoothness-smoothness conditions, encompassing Lasso and gradient Lasso techniques. Experimental results for a specific type of inverse problem show that the dual gradient method outperforms other methods in recovering data in high-dimensional spaces. The research offers a novel contribution to existing theories and opens up potential real-world applications.

Light field imaging, which reconstructs the interaction of light, is highly sensitive to the process of light propagation. However, this sensitive nature creates ambiguities in the process of deriving depth information, as different points along the process may experience occlusions. As a result, most current approaches to extracting depth information from light fields assume a straightforward, nonoccluded process and use metrics that are inherently tied to specific light field paths. Consequently, they often fail to effectively use information from the edges of captured light field images. In order to overcome the limitation of these traditional metrics, we suggest the use of a metric that is more dynamically responsive to the geometry of the captured light field. The Occlusion-Aware Cost Builder is a versatile, modifiable component that can be integrated into any light field disambiguation framework as an alternative to conventional metrics. We also introduce a comprehensive, modifiable framework for deriving depth information from light fields, referred to as Occlusion-Aware Light Field Disambiguation. This framework comprises the Oculation-Aware Cost Builder, a process for block-based matching, and a depth calculation component. In our study, we utilize this framework as an example, incorporating the Oculation-Aware Cost Builder into a state-of-the-art light field disambiguation framework. In our analysis, we compare the performance of this integrated framework with both the original framework and other disambiguation frameworks that utilize other metrics. This study uses the bilinear method to investigate the Fokas-Lenells equations, which initially arise from combining the Maxwell-Bloch equations with the nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger equation. Two particular types of equations are examined: FL-1 and FL-2. For FL-1, we discover a newly identified highly efficient algebraic criterion for N-soliton solutions; in addition, by applying the Frey-Hall residue technique, we derive explicit expressions of multi-soliton solutions and use the Fokas-Lenells mapping to obtain solutions to the Maxwell-Bloch equations. Meanwhile, for FL-2, we employ the Fokas-Lenells mapping after simplifying the equations and derive explicit expressions of N-soliton solutions using the bilinear form of the reduced equations; in addition, we discover a property of N-soliton solutions that exhibit periodic behavior in the temporal variable.

Non-linear links between space and time dimensions are manifested in non-Riemannian actions of gravity,, which, despite their significant implications, have yet to be extensively explored in the context of loop quantum gravity due to the absence of a direct representation in the canonical form of the Hamiltonian. Our approach utilizes double field theory to construct actions describing both Riemannian and non-Riemannian scenarios using a $f(Q,g)$ formulation. By incorporating non-Riemannian contributions from dust-like matter fields, which decouple from the gravitational sector when their momenta are non-constantly canonically transformed, we demonstrate that such actions can be expressed in an simplified form. Our results provide a potential gateway for developing novel quantum gravity models, which may encompass non-Riemannian features and are compatible with the principles of loop quantum gravity.

To improve the performance and efficiency of IEEE 802.11 home WiFi networks, a major issue needs to be addressed – interference caused by repeated transmission within the network. These performance drops can be mitigated by utilizing the backhaul capabilities of IEEE 802.11k/v standards, which enable real-time monitoring of WiFi network assets and dynamics. Our objective is to develop a service offloading strategy for IEEE 802.11 home WiFi networks that takes into account real-time network assets and dynamics. This strategy will minimize the impact of suboptimal AP-to-Extender links, reduce interference in the network, and improve overall network efficiency. By leveraging the capabilities of IEEE 802.11k/v, our approach enables the monitoring of physical and logical links within the network, adjusting the AP and Extender positions accordingly. The performance of our proposed method has been validated through simulations, demonstrating significant improvements in network efficiency compared to non-intelligent selection methods.
